real-time-systems-q1.testing: whether you answer with a chain of stages and owners, not one number.
real-time-systems-q1.spoken:
"Humans leave gaps of roughly 200 to 300 ms between turns. Past about 800 ms a pause reads as lag, and past a second and a half people start talking over it. So I'd set a target like 800 ms at p95 from the moment the user stops to the first sound back, and treat it as a chain rather than a number.

The chain is: deciding the user has finished, getting the final transcript to the logic, deciding what to say, the time to the first token if a model generates it, the time to the first audio byte from TTS, and the network and jitter buffer back to the user. Every hop adds, so the design question is always what can overlap or move before the clock starts.

Two slices usually dominate. Endpointing — how long you wait to be sure they've finished — is a choice, not a constant, and often the biggest. And generation plus synthesis: model time to first token and TTS first byte.

In our interview platform the target is 450 ms at p50 and 800 at p95. The design budget is 150 to 250 for turn detection, about 20 ms of our own logic, 300 for TTS first byte, and 60 to 120 of network: about 530 typical and 690 at p95. No model generation is in it: that happens while the candidate is still talking."

stages.name: The human number
stages.html:
• Natural turn gaps ~200–300 ms; ~800 ms reads as lag; ~1.5 s invites talk-over (conversation-analysis findings, rounded).
  • Quote shape, not false precision: "sub-second, with endpointing and generation as the two levers."

stages.name: Budget is a chain
stages.html: endpoint decision → transcript → decide → (LLM first token) → TTS first byte → network + jitter → ear

stages.name: Where it goes
stages.html:
Prove it — sum the stages (run with Python 3):

stages = {"turn detection": (150, 250), "transcript→agent": (5, 5), "Chair select": (10, 10),
          "TTS dispatch": (5, 5), "TTS first byte": (300, 300), "SFU+network+jitter": (60, 120)}
lo = sum(a for a, _ in stages.values()); hi = sum(b for _, b in stages.values())
print(lo, hi, f"{(250 + 300) / hi:.0%}")   # → 530 690 80%

Two vendor-bound stages are 80% of the p95.

stages.name: The two levers
stages.html:
Lever Move it by
endpointing a semantic end-of-turn model instead of a long fixed silence
generation move it before the endpoint (speculation), stream it, or drop it from the turn
TTS first byte sentence chunking, warm connections, nearest region

followUps.question: p50 or p95?
followUps.html: Both, per turn. Users remember the slow turns; p95 is the one the product feels. Averages per session hide the tail.

followUps.question: "Humans pause a second between turns, so a second is fine."
followUps.html: Typical gaps are a few hundred ms. A second of silence after a direct question reads as the system not having heard.

followUps.question: 🧪 TTS first byte goes from 300 to 450 ms. What's the p95?
followUps.html: 690 − 300 + 450 = 840 ms, over the 800 ms target on arithmetic alone.

followUps.question: Who owns the budget?
followUps.html: It's a product requirement with engineering owners per stage. Most of it sits with vendors, so the owner's job is vendor selection and verification under load, not only code.

dontSay: One total with no stages.
An LLM call inside the budget without saying how it's hidden.

real-time-systems-q2.testing: that you optimise time to first audio, not total response time, and that you measure it at the right percentile.
real-time-systems-q2.trap: optimising end-to-end completion time while the first sound is still slow.
real-time-systems-q2.spoken:
"The user feels time to first audio: the silence between when they stop talking and when they hear the first sound back. They hear the start of a reply, not the end, so total generation time barely matters as long as audio keeps flowing once it starts.

That's why everything streams. The first TTS chunk plays while the model is still generating, and TTS starts on the first sentence, not the whole reply. In our system we split the text at sentence ends or every 12 words, and give each segment its own TTS stream, which took first audio on a long unpunctuated sentence from 677 to 437 ms.

Perceived latency can also be shaped. A short, honest acknowledgement buys real time. Our design calls it a bridge utterance — 'That's useful, let me build on that' — and it buys about a second and a half without dead air. What we don't do is fake it with synthesised 'um's: once candidates know it's a system, that reads as manipulative.

I measure p95 of first audio per turn, not average end-to-end per session. Total duration matters for cost and for barge-in, not for the feel."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html: • Felt latency = end of user speech → first audio byte heard. In our requirement: endpoint → first TTS byte (N1).

stages.name: Why first audio, not completion
stages.html:
Metric Felt? Matters for
first audio yes the conversation
full reply duration no (while audio flows) cost, barge-in window
a gap mid-reply yes, badly chunk sizing and pacing

stages.name: How to shape it
stages.html:
Prove it — first audio on a 32-word unpunctuated sentence ( 24 Sep 2026, warm, Deepgram TTS from India):

Path First audio
one TTS stream for the reply 677 ms
12-word forced flush, one stream per segment 437 ms
  • Bridge utterance (): honest content that buys ~1.5 s; filler injection is banned by design.

stages.name: What to measure
stages.html: • endpoint_to_first_byte_ms{quantile} per turn; the prototype logs e2e, llm_ttft and tts_ttfb per agent turn.

stages.name: Where it bites
stages.claim: the first turn and the tail
stages.html:
• First turn: cold connections (~620 ms TLS to the TTS vendor from India) unless opened before speech.
  • Tail: vendor queueing under load shows up at p95 first.

followUps.question: Why not a filler word to buy time?
followUps.html: It works on people who think they're talking to a person. An AI interviewer that says "um" reads as manipulative once candidates know. A bridge line with real content is the honest version.

followUps.question: How small can the first chunk be?
followUps.html: Small enough to start fast, large enough for natural prosody. A sentence or a clause is right; a fixed token count gives flat or broken intonation. The 12-word cap only bounds the worst case.

followUps.question: 🧪 First audio is 400 ms but users still say it feels slow. Where do you look?
followUps.html: Gaps between chunks (next segment not ready), the endpoint wait before the clock you're measuring starts, and the first turn's cold connect. Measure from the user's last word, not from your endpoint event.

dontSay: "Total response time is what matters."

real-time-systems-q3.testing: whether you know which work can move before the endpoint, and that every overlap trades wasted compute for latency.
real-time-systems-q3.trap: a strict STT → LLM → TTS chain, then blaming the models for being slow.
real-time-systems-q3.spoken:
"The principle: anything that can happen while the user is still talking shouldn't be on the clock after they stop.

Streaming STT gives interim transcripts every few hundred ms. You can start work on those: in our system, each final phrase triggers the analysis agents — scoring, gap-finding, integrity — debounced and restarted as the answer grows, so an insight is usually ready at the endpoint. The design goes further with speculative pre-generation: draft two to four candidate next questions during speech, fully rendered, and at the endpoint just pick one in about 10 ms. The prototype uses LiveKit's preemptive generation, a cheaper version: start the reply on the transcript before the end of turn is confirmed and throw it away if they keep talking.

Then overlap generation with synthesis: chunk the text at sentence boundaries, or every 12 words, and start a TTS stream per chunk immediately, so the first sentence plays while the rest is generated.

And keep everything warm: connections to STT and TTS open before the first word, models loaded before the job arrives. A cold TLS connect to our TTS vendor from India was about 620 ms.

Every overlap spends some compute that gets discarded. Speculation is 2–3× the tokens; that's the price of feeling like one fast interviewer."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
chained:     speech ──► endpoint ──► STT final ──► LLM ──► TTS ──► audio
overlapped:  speech ──► endpoint ──► pick ──► TTS(first sentence) ──► audio
             └─ interims ─► analysis, drafts ─┘       └─ rest of reply keeps generating

stages.name: Speculate on partials
stages.html:
Speculative pre-generation Preemptive generation
When continuously during speech once end-of-turn looks likely
Output 2–4 ranked NextMoves with confidence one reply
At endpoint Chair picks in ~10 ms, staleness check used if the transcript didn't change
Waste 2–3× tokens a discarded reply when speech continues

stages.name: Stream into TTS
stages.html:
Prove it — how the chunker splits a long question (run with Python 3):

import re
END = re.compile(r"[.!?…]['\")\]]*$")
def segments(words, max_words=12):
    seg = []
    for w in words:
        seg.append(w)
        if END.search(w) or len(seg) >= max_words:
            yield " ".join(seg); seg = []
    if seg: yield " ".join(seg)
text = ("Walk me through how you would shard the ledger table when one tenant "
        "writes ten times more than the rest and reads must stay consistent. Take your time.")
for s in segments(text.split()): print(len(s.split()), "|", s)
# → 12 | Walk me through how you would shard the ledger table when one
# → 12 | tenant writes ten times more than the rest and reads must stay
# → 1 | consistent.
# → 3 | Take your time.

The first 12 words go to TTS without waiting for the full stop. The one-word tail is the cost of a forced flush.

stages.name: Keep everything warm
stages.claim: no cold starts on the clock
stages.html:
• STT socket open before first speech; TTS connections pooled; VAD loaded in prewarm.
  • Harness lesson: abandoning a stream midway discarded its pooled connection, and TTS read 1.3 s instead of 319 ms.

stages.name: What it costs
stages.html: • Discarded drafts and replies are paid tokens. If the unit economics hurt, generate fewer candidates, don't stop speculating.

followUps.question: When is a partial safe to act on?
followUps.html: For drafting and analysis, any time: they're discardable. For side effects (a tool call, a transfer, a record), only on the final transcript. See Q8.

followUps.question: "Speculation doubles the cost; not worth it."
followUps.html: It's the only way to keep generation off the clock when a model's first token alone is ~850 ms. The trade is explicit; the knob is how many candidates, not whether.

followUps.question: 🧪 The user adds a sentence after the preemptive reply was generated. What's spoken?
followUps.html: Nothing from that reply. The turn wasn't committed, so it's discarded and the brain runs again on the longer transcript. Because graph writes are keyed by turn and overwritten, there's still one decision per turn in the record.

dontSay: "We wait for the final transcript, then call the LLM."

real-time-systems-q4.testing: whether you separate true physical limits from things that only look fixed, and whether region placement is on your list.
real-time-systems-q4.trap: treating model load or cold connections as part of the floor.
real-time-systems-q4.spoken:
"The true floor is physics plus framing. Light in fibre covers roughly 200 km per millisecond, and real routes are longer than straight lines, so an intercontinental round trip is tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds and no engineering removes it. That makes region placement a latency decision: media, inference and TTS should sit near the user. In our design, for an Indian product, regional versus distant is roughly 15 ms versus 90 ms, which is 13% of the turn budget spent before any work.

Then audio framing: frames are 10 to 20 ms, and the jitter buffer on the listener's side holds a few frames to smooth network variance. That's inherent buffering, 60 to 120 ms together with the network in our budget.

What people call a floor but isn't: model load time, cold TLS handshakes, autoscaling from zero. Those are avoidable with warm pools and prewarmed processes. Our cold connect to the TTS vendor from India was about 620 ms on the first turn only, because after that the connection is pooled.

So: state the floor out loud, then show what you optimise above it."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html: • Propagation delay (distance), plus the minimum buffering real-time audio needs.

stages.name: Physics: distance
stages.html:
Prove it — back-of-envelope (light in fibre ≈ 200 km/ms; routes longer than great circles):

Mumbai ↔ Singapore   ~3,900 km  → ≥ ~39 ms round trip on fibre physics alone
Mumbai ↔ US East     ~13,000 km → ≥ ~130 ms round trip
our design note: regional ~15 ms vs distant ~90 ms → 13% of a ~700 ms budget

stages.name: Framing and buffering
stages.html:
Item Typical
Opus frame 10–20 ms
jitter buffer a few frames, adaptive; deeper = smoother + later
SFU forward a few ms (no transcoding)

stages.name: The avoidable "floor"
stages.html:
Looks fixed Fix
model load (VAD, turn model) prewarm per process before jobs arrive
TLS to vendors (~620 ms cold, ) open and pool before first speech
scale from zero keep warm capacity for live sessions

followUps.question: Your LLM vendor has no Indian region. Now what?
followUps.html: Keep its calls off the clock (speculation during speech), or pick a provider with nearer capacity for the latency-critical calls and keep the far one for post-call scoring.

followUps.question: "5G and fibre make distance irrelevant."
followUps.html: They lower last-mile latency and jitter; they don't change the speed of light between regions.

followUps.question: 🧪 Candidates in the US join your India-hosted interview. What's the extra cost per turn?
followUps.html: At least one extra long-haul leg on the downlink, on the order of 100+ ms at p95 (illustrative). Enough to make an 800 ms p95 marginal; a second region is the fix.

dontSay: "Model loading is our floor."

spine: It's a session, not a request
real-time-systems-q5.testing: the stages in order, the control loops running beside them, and where state lives.
real-time-systems-q5.trap: describing a request/response API. The state and the interruption loop are the hard parts.
real-time-systems-q5.spoken:
"First framing: this is a long-lived, stateful session, not a request/response service. Every stage streams, and every stage has its own timeout and fallback.

In order: the browser captures the mic with echo cancellation, noise suppression and gain control on; audio goes as Opus over WebRTC to a LiveKit SFU, which forwards it without transcoding to the agent's job process. There, Krisp noise cancellation cleans the input; Silero VAD says whether there's speech; Deepgram streaming STT turns it into interim and final transcripts, with keyterms for the interview's vocabulary; and LiveKit's turn-detection model decides whether the candidate has finished or is pausing. When the turn commits, the brain runs — rules pick the move, a speaker agent phrases it — and the text goes to TTS in sentence-sized chunks. The audio goes back through the SFU to the candidate.

Two control loops run beside it. Barge-in: if the candidate speaks while the agent is talking, the agent stops within about half a second and the record keeps only what was heard. And turn state: who holds the floor, what was actually delivered, where the plan is.

The split of ownership: LiveKit owns audio, VAD, turn detection and interruption mechanics; we own everything where an audio event has a scoring consequence — echo, vocabulary, truncation bookkeeping, degradation.

Everything is observed per turn: end-of-turn delay, STT delay, model first token, TTS first byte and end-to-end."

stages.name: It's a session, not a request
stages.html: • One process per interview holds the plan, the delivered moves, the analysis results and the connections.

stages.name: The audio path, in order
The two control loops
stages.html:
Loop Trigger Owner
barge-in ≥ 0.4 s of voice while the agent speaks LiveKit mechanics, our bookkeeping
false interruption no words within 2 s → resume LiveKit
turn state committed turns, delivered moves ours (event-sourced)

stages.name: Who owns what
stages.html:
LiveKit Ours
Opus, jitter buffer, ICE, TURN, reconnection device check, echo semantics + guard
VAD, turn detection, interruption mechanics rubric-derived vocabulary, pronunciation lexicon
STT/TTS plugin invocation, process per session truncation bookkeeping, degradation policy, fairness measurement

stages.name: Per-turn observability
stages.html:
Prove it — what one turn logs ( format):

USER  '<answer>' | stt_delay=… eou_delay=…
CHAIR turn=4 intent=answer → probe q=1 (prober: no numbers on throughput) [0.4ms, insight=ready]
AGENT '<reply>' | e2e=… llm_ttft=… tts_ttfb=…

followUps.question: Where is barge-in handled?
followUps.html: Detection and audio flushing in LiveKit Agents, on VAD. The record and the plan consequences in our code. See Q34.

followUps.question: What's checkpointed and why?
followUps.html: Chair's move per turn, keyed and overwritten, so a preemptive re-run is idempotent and evaluation can read what was decided. Durable data goes to Postgres in background tasks.

followUps.question: What happens on a provider 500?
followUps.html: The breaker counts it; after five it opens and calls fail fast into the fallback: secondary TTS voice, skipped analysis, or scripted mode. See Q46.

followUps.question: "It's just STT, LLM, TTS."
followUps.html: That's the data path. Endpointing, interruption, echo, vocabulary and degradation are where the product lives and where it breaks.

dontSay: A three-box diagram with no control loops.

real-time-systems-q6.testing: that you separate VAD, endpointing and turn detection, and treat the threshold as the biggest tunable slice of the budget.
real-time-systems-q6.spoken:
"It's three questions, not one. VAD asks whether there's speech in this 30 ms frame. Endpointing asks whether this utterance has ended. Turn detection asks whether the person has finished their turn, or is pausing to think.

A fixed silence threshold forces a bad trade: 150 ms interrupts anyone who pauses mid-thought, 500 ms still cuts some people off and makes the agent feel slow. So the better approach is semantic: a model that reads the last few turns of text alongside the audio. 'I'd shard by tenant.' is complete; 'I used Kubernetes for the…' isn't, even after the same pause.

We use LiveKit's end-of-turn model for that, with Silero VAD underneath and the STT vendor's own endpointing switched off, so there's only one authority. The settings are a minimum wait of 0.8 seconds when the turn sounds finished and up to 3.5 seconds when the model thinks they're mid-thought. We started at 0.5 and it cut answers at thinking pauses.

Where it breaks: noise and accents. Noise can make VAD see speech that isn't there, and the turn model is English-only by its vendor's statement, so cut-off rates need measuring per accent. Cutting off a thinker is a fairness problem in an interview, not just UX."

stages.name: Three different questions
stages.html:
Question Time scale
VAD speech in this frame? ~30 ms frames, ~1 ms each (Silero)
endpointing utterance ended? hundreds of ms of silence
turn detection turn ended? words + prosody, ~50 ms model inference

stages.name: Why a silence timer fails
stages.html:
Threshold Effect
150 ms interrupts thinkers
250 ms still cuts mid-sentence pauses
500 ms+ never interrupts, feels dead

stages.name: How a semantic model decides
stages.html:
• LiveKit's model: a small transformer (135M params, SmolLM v2 base), sliding window of recent turns, predicts "end of utterance" probability (LiveKit).
  • The wait adapts: short when the text looks complete, long when it doesn't.

Prove it — the prototype's settings ():

turn_detection = LiveKit TurnDetector (audio + words)
endpointing    = min_delay 0.8 s (was 0.5: cut thinking pauses), max_delay 3.5 s
stt            = endpointing_ms 0 (off); plugin sends Finalize when VAD ends speech

stages.name: Tuning it
stages.html:
• end_of_turn_delay per turn; manual case V-22 ("The main challenge was… (1.5 s pause) …keeping ordering per account" must be one turn).
  • Context helps: after "my policy number is…" a long pause is expected; a semantic model gets much of that from the words.

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
• Noise → false speech frames; Krisp BVC and browser NS reduce them.
  • Accent → the model's training distribution; validate per cohort.
  • A live split: "I'm Prathap, a / pen engineer" — "backend" lost at the break. The agent treats the split answer as one answer, so the cost is a restarted reply, not a skipped question.

followUps.question: Why not STT endpointing, like the vendor recommends?
followUps.html: LiveKit itself recommends it as the default. We deviate because interviews have long thinking pauses, and a semantic model handles them better; two endpointing authorities would fight. See Q33.

followUps.question: "VAD tells you when they're done."
followUps.html: VAD tells you there's silence now. Whether the silence means "done" is the turn-detection question.

followUps.question: 🧪 min_delay 0.8 s → 0.5 s. What happens to latency and cut-offs?
followUps.html: Up to 300 ms faster on finished-sounding turns, and more cut-offs at thinking pauses: exactly what we saw before raising it.

dontSay: "500 ms silence timeout" as the design.

spine: Not every sound is a turn
real-time-systems-q7.testing: the full mechanism — detection, cancellation of audio and generation, history reconciliation, false positives — not just "we stop talking".
real-time-systems-q7.trap: logging the full generated reply into history when the user heard four words of it.
real-time-systems-q7.spoken:
"That's barge-in, and the agent should yield immediately — finishing the sentence reads as rude and robotic.

Detection has to be acoustic. Voice activity detection fires on the user's voice within a few hundred ms; the transcript would arrive 200 to 300 ms later, by which point the agent has spoken over them. In our system it's LiveKit's VAD mode: 0.4 seconds of voice while the agent is speaking.

Then stop everything upstream, not just the speaker: stop consuming the TTS stream, flush the audio already queued for sending, and cancel the model generation, or you pay for tokens nobody hears.

Then reconcile state. The conversation history must record what the user actually heard, truncated and marked interrupted, not what was generated. Otherwise the next turn assumes they heard things they didn't. In an interview product it goes further: a question they only half-heard can't count as asked, and their answer can't be scored against it.

Not every sound is an interruption. A cough, a door, or a short 'mm-hm' shouldn't stop the agent. We ignore voice under 0.4 seconds and, if no words arrive within two seconds, the agent resumes where it stopped. And echo has to be cancelled first, or the agent barges in on itself."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: yield on sound, record what was heard
stages.html: • Barge-in is the event; interruption handling is the mechanism around it.

stages.name: Detect on sound
stages.html:
Signal Available after Use
VAD onset ~frames (tens of ms) + min duration trigger barge-in
interim transcript ~200–300 ms too late to trigger

interruption = {mode: vad, min_duration: 0.4 s, false_interruption_timeout: 2.0 s}

stages.name: Stop everything upstream
stages.html:
1. Stop consuming the TTS stream.
  2. Flush the outbound pacing buffer (audio already synthesised).
  3. The client's playout ends with the stream.
  4. Cancel generation.

In our system LiveKit Agents owns this sequence; it's easy to get subtly wrong by hand.

stages.name: Record what was heard
stages.html:
Prove it — the history difference (illustrative):

generated : "That makes sense. How would you shard the ledger if one tenant writes ten times more?"
heard     : "That makes sense. How would you shard the led…"          interrupted = true
stored    : the heard version
plan      : the probe didn't happen → no budget spent, same question stays current

stages.name: Not every sound is a turn
stages.html:
Sound Behaviour
"mm-hm" < 0.4 s ignored
cough, no words pause, resume within 2 s, no user turn
the agent's own echo should be removed by AEC; the server echo guard keeps it out of the record

vad mode is predictable; LiveKit's adaptive mode uses a model to ignore backchannels, the production candidate once measured.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
• barge_in_total{source=candidate|suspected_echo}, false-positive rate, truncated characters.
  • Most tuning assumes peers; an interviewer holds the floor longer, so tune for that.

followUps.question: Why not wait for the transcript to check it's a real interruption?
followUps.html: The user would hear the agent talk over them for 200–300 ms. Yield on sound, then decide: resume on no words.

followUps.question: "Just finish the sentence, then listen."
followUps.html: It feels robotic, and in an interview it can drown out the candidate's clarification request.

followUps.question: 🧪 The user says "right, yeah" while the agent explains. Barge-in or not?
followUps.html: It's agreement, not a turn bid. Under 0.4 s it's ignored; longer, vad mode would stop the agent, which is the trade-off against adaptive mode.

followUps.question: Should the agent ever backchannel itself?
followUps.html: Not on a half-duplex pipeline: an "mm-hm" would arrive late and read as an interruption. We buy responsiveness with latency instead.

dontSay: "We stop the TTS" and nothing about history.

real-time-systems-q8.testing: the rule that side effects wait for finals, and that you know partials are revised.
real-time-systems-q8.trap: firing a tool call or a record off a partial that later changes.
real-time-systems-q8.spoken:
"Streaming STT emits interim transcripts every few hundred ms — fast, but revisable: the model can change earlier words as more audio arrives. Then it emits a final for a phrase, which is stable.

Partials are for responsiveness: live captions, early intent, and speculative work that can be thrown away. Finals are for commitment: anything with a side effect, like a tool call, a record, a transfer, waits for the final. A decision you'd regret if the words changed must not be made on a partial.

Confidence gates action: low confidence on something high-stakes means confirm, not act.

In our system, Deepgram sends interims about every 300 ms and they drive the live captions and LiveKit's preemptive generation, which is discardable. The analysis agents trigger on final phrases, which Deepgram emits before the end of the turn is decided, debounced 300 ms. The candidate's turn is committed only when the turn detector says they're done, and only then is it written to the transcript and used by Chair. STT confidence is used only to ask for a repeat and never reaches the scorer, for fairness."

stages.name: What each one is
stages.html:
Interim (partial) Final
Cadence ~300 ms per phrase / on finalize
Stability revisable stable
Right for captions, drafts, early signals records, tool calls, scoring

stages.name: Partials for responsiveness
stages.html: • Captions to the browser (text streams), preemptive generation (discarded if speech continues).

stages.name: Finals for commitment
stages.claim: and one more level above them
stages.html:
Prove it — three levels in our pipeline ():

interim       ~300 ms     → captions, preemptive reply (discardable)
final phrase  mid-answer  → T1 analysis, debounced 300 ms, restarted on the next phrase
committed turn (EOU)      → transcript store, Chair's move, persisted insight

stages.name: Confidence gates action
stages.html:
• High stakes + low confidence → read back and confirm (see Q20).
  • Sustained stt_confidence < 0.6 → ask to repeat, then offer text fallback.

stages.name: How we use them
stages.claim: and what we don't pass on
stages.html: • stt_confidence never leaves the STT layer: it isn't written to the turn record and isn't visible to the Assessor (N6).

followUps.question: Why not let the scorer see confidence? It's useful.
followUps.html: Confidence varies with accent, so it would carry accent into the score. It's used only for the repeat path.

followUps.question: "Partials are good enough to act on; they're usually right."
followUps.html: "Usually" is the problem: the revision cases are exactly the ambiguous words, often the ones that matter (names, numbers).

followUps.question: 🧪 A partial says "fifteen", the final says "fifty". What went wrong if an action fired?
followUps.html: The action was bound to a partial. The fix is structural: actions subscribe to committed turns only.

dontSay: "We act on the partial to save time."

spine: Chunk on boundaries, bound the worst case
real-time-systems-q9.testing: that you chunk on linguistic boundaries for prosody, bound the first chunk for latency, and fix pronunciation before synthesis.
real-time-systems-q9.trap: chunking by fixed token count, or waiting for the whole reply.
real-time-systems-q9.spoken:
"Stream at sentence granularity. Synthesis needs a complete phrase for natural intonation, so chunk on sentence or clause boundaries — but bound the worst case, because models sometimes produce a long sentence with no punctuation, and an unbounded first chunk puts the whole generation back on the clock. We flush at sentence end or every 12 words.

Each segment gets its own TTS stream, started as soon as the segment exists, so segment one is being synthesised and played while segment two is still being generated. With pooled connections, per-segment streams are cheap.

Before synthesis, normalise the text. Tokens arrive split mid-word, so only complete words are released; then a pronunciation lexicon maps terms like k8s to 'Kubernetes' and etcd to 'E T C D'. The transcript keeps the original text.

Measured: on a 32-word unpunctuated sentence, first audio went from 677 ms with one stream to 437 with the 12-word flush. Fixed phrases like greetings and closings could be cached entirely."

stages.html:
• LiveKit's Deepgram TTS flushes only at the end of the whole reply; a long first sentence would hold back the first byte.

followUps.question: Why complete words only?
followUps.html: Tokens split words ("Postgre" + "SQL"). Releasing half a word breaks both synthesis and the lexicon match.

followUps.question: "Chunk every N tokens; it's simpler."
followUps.html: It cuts phrases mid-clause and flattens prosody. Boundaries first, the count only as a cap.

followUps.question: 🧪 A 13-word sentence with a full stop at the end. How many segments?
followUps.html: Two: the first 12 words (forced flush), then the last word with its full stop. A one-word tail can sound clipped; prompts that ask for short sentences avoid it.

spine: Where the line falls for us
real-time-systems-q10.testing: whether you can weigh a trending technology against control, observability and compliance, without dismissing it.
real-time-systems-q10.trap: presenting speech-to-speech as a pure upgrade, or dismissing it as a toy.
real-time-systems-q10.spoken:
"Not for us today, and the reason is specific to what we're building.

Native speech-to-speech models take audio in and produce audio out, so they remove the STT, LLM and TTS hops. That wins latency, and it keeps prosody, tone and emotion that a transcript throws away. For a conversational assistant that's a real upgrade.

What the cascade keeps is control and a record. In an interview product, the transcript is the evidence: every score has to cite what the candidate said, verbatim, and a human has to be able to review it. The cascade also gives us per-stage control where our product lives: keyterm prompting so technical terms survive, a pronunciation lexicon, an echo guard that drops our own voice before the record, and a rules-based Chair that decides which question comes next so the model can't be talked out of the plan. And each stage is swappable and measurable on its own goldens.

So the honest 2026 answer is hybrid by path. Speech-to-speech could carry the conversational layer if it can be constrained to speak the planned question verbatim, while a parallel STT keeps the transcript of record and the scoring stays on text. What would change my mind: if our turn budget can't be met with the cascade under load, the pipeline shape itself is the problem."

followUps.question: Isn't the prosody information valuable for assessment?
followUps.html: For an interviewer it's exactly what we must not use: confidence of tone correlates with accent, culture and nerves, not competence. N6 forbids scoring signal from voice.

followUps.question: What about tool calling with speech-to-speech?
followUps.html: Improving across vendors (as of 2026), but anything that acts should still act on a committed transcript and structured output, which pushes those paths back to text.

followUps.question: 🧪 Regulator asks for the exact words of question 3 and the candidate's answer. Which architecture answers faster?
followUps.html: The cascade: the planned question text is stored verbatim with its delivered flag, and the answer is the committed transcript. With speech-to-speech alone you'd be transcribing recorded audio after the fact.

real-time-systems-q11.testing: that you choose by path — user's browser vs server-to-server — and can name head-of-line blocking.
real-time-systems-q11.trap: WebSockets for browser mic audio, then debugging jitter you have no tools for.
real-time-systems-q11.spoken:
"It depends on the path. Real user audio over the public internet: WebRTC. Server-to-server audio where you control both ends and the network is good: a WebSocket is fine.

The reason is TCP. A WebSocket runs on TCP, which must deliver every byte in order, so one lost packet stalls everything behind it — head-of-line blocking. For live speech you'd rather drop a 20 ms frame and conceal it than stall and then burst.

WebRTC is UDP-based and built for media: a jitter buffer, packet-loss concealment, Opus with adaptive bitrate, ICE for getting through NATs, encryption, and — the one that decided it for us — browser-native echo cancellation, which only works on the capture path the browser controls.

The cost is complexity: signalling, ICE, STUN and TURN, more to operate. We took that complexity off our hands with LiveKit.

In our system both are used: WebRTC between the candidate and the SFU and agent, and WebSockets from the agent to Deepgram for STT and TTS, which is a controlled server-to-server path from inside the region."

Path Choose

telephony SIP/PSTN, with its own codecs

followUps.question: What about WebTransport or QUIC?
followUps.html: QUIC removes TCP's head-of-line blocking across streams and supports datagrams, so it's promising for media. But you still rebuild jitter buffering, concealment and AEC. For browser voice today, WebRTC is the mature choice.

followUps.question: "WebSockets are real-time."
followUps.html: They're low-latency when nothing is lost. The problem is the behaviour under loss, which is exactly when real networks hurt.

followUps.question: 🧪 1% packet loss on a residential link. Which transport degrades more gracefully?
followUps.html: WebRTC: 1 in 100 frames concealed, mostly inaudible. TCP: a stall of about one round trip each time, heard as stutter and growing delay.

dontSay: "WebRTC is peer-to-peer, so it doesn't fit a server agent." (An SFU or agent is just another peer.)

spine: How it looks with an SFU
real-time-systems-q12.testing: the order of the handshake, and that you know a real share of calls ends up relayed.
real-time-systems-q12.trap: calling WebRTC peer-to-peer and forgetting TURN.
real-time-systems-q12.spoken:
"Four phases. Signalling first, and it isn't part of WebRTC: the two sides exchange an SDP offer and answer over a channel you provide, describing the media, codecs and encryption fingerprints.

Then ICE gathers candidate addresses: host addresses on the local interface, server-reflexive addresses discovered through STUN — your public address as a NAT sees it — and relay addresses on a TURN server. Candidates are trickled to the other side through signalling.

Then connectivity checks: ICE tries candidate pairs and picks one that works, preferring direct paths and falling back to TURN, which always works because it relays every byte, and always costs for the same reason. Some NATs and firewalls block UDP entirely, so TURN over TCP or TLS on 443 is the last resort.

Once a pair is chosen, a DTLS handshake sets up keys and SRTP carries the encrypted media. Mid-call, a network change — wifi to cellular — triggers an ICE restart.

With LiveKit it's the same protocol but a simpler shape: the client connects to the SFU over a signalling WebSocket with a token, negotiates with the SFU rather than with the agent, and the agent is another participant. LiveKit's built-in TURN covers the clients that can't reach the SFU directly."

followUps.question: STUN vs TURN?
followUps.html: STUN tells you your public address; it carries no media. TURN relays media when no direct path works.

followUps.question: "WebRTC is peer-to-peer, so no server cost."
followUps.html: Signalling always needs a server, a real share of calls need TURN, and any multi-party or server-side agent design uses an SFU.

followUps.question: 🧪 A corporate network blocks all UDP. Does the call work?
followUps.html: Only via TURN over TCP/TLS on 443, which WebRTC and LiveKit support. It works with higher latency and head-of-line effects; monitor that path separately.

dontSay: "Signalling is part of WebRTC."

spine: Why TURN costs what it costs
Cut the cost per relayed minute
real-time-systems-q13.testing: that you plan TURN on concurrent relayed bandwidth, measure the relay ratio, and know the operational lessons (spot nodes, region).
real-time-systems-q13.trap: capacity planning on registered users, or saying "we just used a managed TURN".
real-time-systems-q13.spoken:
"TURN relays every byte of a call for clients that can't reach you directly, so it's priced by bandwidth and scales with concurrent relayed minutes, not with users. The number I watch is the relay ratio: the share of sessions whose selected ICE pair is a relay.

First I cut the rate: correct STUN so clients discover their public address, IPv6 where possible, and making sure the media server itself is reachable directly on UDP, so only clients behind restrictive NATs or firewalls relay. Then the cost per relayed minute: region-local relays, and self-hosting where the volume justifies it.

In our case, the earlier stack was WebRTC with a self-hosted coturn relay, and it taught us one hard rule: anything holding live media state doesn't run on spot nodes — an evicted relay drops live calls, and an interview can't be re-run. When we moved to LiveKit, the SFU took the relay's place in the path and its built-in TURN covers the clients that can't reach it directly, so we stopped running coturn as a separate system. It's all in one Indian region, on on-demand nodes.

The numbers: <fill: relay ratio and cost per relayed minute, before → after>."

Opus audio ≈ 40 kbps per direction per track (with overhead)
one relayed interview = up + down ≈ 80 kbps through the relay (in and out ≈ 2× on the relay's NIC)
1,000 concurrent × 20% relayed = 200 relayed calls ≈ 16 Mbps each way — cheap for audio
the same maths for 720p video (~1.5 Mbps) is ~40× more

For audio-only, TURN cost is modest; its operational risk (placement, eviction, region) matters more.

real-time-systems-q14.testing: that you design the degraded path — including a degraded transcript — not just the clean one.
real-time-systems-q14.trap: stopping at "the jitter buffer handles it".
real-time-systems-q14.spoken:
"In layers. First the media stack absorbs it: the jitter buffer grows to smooth timing variance, which adds a little latency; packet-loss concealment fills lost frames; Opus lowers its bitrate; and redundant encoding helps with bursts. A few percent loss is mostly inaudible. LiveKit owns all of that.

Second, the transcript degrades before the audio sounds bad: recognition confidence drops and words go missing. That's the part people forget, and in an interview it's a scoring problem. So the agent confirms more: a low-confidence turn gets a repeat request rather than being treated as a vague answer.

Third, the interview adapts. If quality stays poor, the agent acknowledges the line, slows its pacing and offers text: the candidate can finish the interview by typing. That's a first-class path, not an error: the transcript is valid, the scoring works on text, and the scorecard records the modality so a human can weigh it. Rescheduling costs the candidate a day; typing the last ten minutes costs very little.

If the connection drops, LiveKit reconnects and the interview state survives in the job process. If it can't reconnect, we save the turns, score the partial transcript, and offer to resume from the next question."

followUps.question: Is a typed answer comparable to a spoken one?
followUps.html: Not obviously: typing gives time to think and edit. That's why the scorecard records the modality; whether it needs a scoring caveat is an open question we'd answer with data.

followUps.question: What happens on wifi → cellular?
followUps.html: An ICE restart onto the new network; a short gap covered by the jitter buffer and a bridge line if it lasts. The session and its state don't change.

followUps.question: 🧪 Loss is 8% in bursts. What does the candidate hear, and what does the scorer see?

real-time-systems-q15.testing: that you rank bottlenecks for a stateful, long-lived workload and know provider quotas bite before your own infra.
real-time-systems-q15.trap: autoscaling on CPU and killing pods mid-call on every deploy.
real-time-systems-q15.spoken:
"Voice sessions are stateful and long-lived, so the stateless autoscaling playbook doesn't apply: you can't move a live call to another pod, and a killed pod drops it.

In our planning the order is: vendor concurrency and cost break first. At 1000 concurrent calls you hold 1000 streams each to STT, TTS and the LLM. If the TTS vendor starts queueing at a few hundred streams, first-audio latency climbs for everyone, and our TTS first byte is 55% of the turn budget. Second, the SFU topology: 2000 audio tracks is cheap bandwidth, but past a single node's comfortable limits, so it needs multi-node with Redis. Third, event-loop lag inside each call's process — a blocking call shows up as dead air. Last, and most boring, node CPU and memory: linear and easy to buy.

How it shows up: p95 first audio drifting up with concurrency while CPU stays low means a vendor is queueing you. Dispatch wait growing means the worker fleet is short. Loop-lag alerts mean a code problem, not a capacity one.

What never to do: scale on CPU, scale from zero, or kill pods on deploy. Scale on concurrent sessions, keep warm capacity, and drain for the length of a call."

real-time-systems-q16.testing: backpressure for a producer you can't slow down, and whether you pick an overflow policy on purpose.
real-time-systems-q16.trap: an unbounded queue ("it'll catch up"), which becomes memory growth, growing lag and then an OOM.
real-time-systems-q16.spoken:
"Audio is a real-time producer you can't pause: the person keeps talking whatever your consumer is doing. So the first rule is a bounded buffer with an explicit overflow policy. Unbounded means memory grows, lag grows with it, and eventually the process is killed.

The policy depends on where you are. For audio headed to a live decision, stale audio is worthless: if you're 2 seconds behind, you'd rather drop the oldest frames and catch up than process the backlog perfectly and reply late. For audio headed to a record — the transcript of an interview — dropping loses evidence, so you'd rather apply backpressure upstream or spill to a durable buffer.

In the Deepgram pipeline I built, the fix was a bounded asyncio.Queue where the producer awaits put(), which throttles it naturally instead of growing memory: <fill: the size N and how you picked it>.

Then degrade deliberately: shed non-critical work first. In our current design that's already built in: the analysis tier has deadlines and a budget, so under pressure it stops and the turn loop keeps going.

And alert on queue depth: a sustained backlog means you're under-provisioned, not momentarily unlucky."

stages.name: The producer can't be paused
stages.html: • 20 ms frames arrive at 50 per second regardless of consumer speed.

stages.name: Bound the buffer
stages.claim: size it in time, not items
stages.html: • A bound of N frames is N × 20 ms of audio; pick it from the latency you can tolerate.

stages.name: Drop stale, don't block
stages.html:
Prove it — drop-oldest on a stalled consumer (run with Python 3):

import asyncio, collections
async def main():
    buf = collections.deque(maxlen=5)          # 5 × 20 ms frames = 100 ms of audio
    dropped = 0
    for frame in range(12):                   # 12 frames arrive while the consumer is stalled
        if len(buf) == buf.maxlen: dropped += 1
        buf.append(frame)
    print(list(buf), "dropped:", dropped)
asyncio.run(main())
# → [7, 8, 9, 10, 11] dropped: 7
Policy Right for Cost
drop oldest live detection, captions lost audio, counted
block producer (await put()) internal stages you can slow pushes delay upstream
spill to durable storage the record complexity, disk

followUps.question: Why drop rather than block?
followUps.html: Blocking the microphone producer doesn't stop the person talking; it moves the backlog into the socket or the OS buffer. For live audio, late is as bad as lost.

followUps.question: "Make the queue bigger."
followUps.html: A bigger queue is more latency and more memory when the consumer is structurally slower. Fix the rate mismatch or shed work.

real-time-systems-q17.testing: detection, timeout, a failover that doesn't restart the call, and an honest spoken fallback.
real-time-systems-q17.trap: a fallback that needs the call restarted and loses the conversation.
real-time-systems-q17.spoken:
"Degraded STT shows up two ways: slow — interims and finals arriving late — or bad — confidence dropping and words vanishing. I watch both per session: the interim interval, final latency, confidence and empty transcripts while VAD says there's speech.

The turn must not hang on it. The STT stream has a timeout and a circuit breaker; if the stream stalls, the turn detector still has VAD, and the agent can say a short bridge line rather than sit in silence.

Failover mid-call is the hard part: the stream handle and the buffered audio have to move. A second provider needs its own warm connection and its own vocabulary list, and you accept losing the words in flight. If there's no second provider, degrade: ask the candidate to repeat, and if the problem persists, offer to continue by typing. The transcript stays valid either way.

Two things I'd keep. The spoken fallback must be honest — 'I'm having trouble hearing you' — not silence. And the record: turns already committed are safe in the database, and the post-call scoring runs on whatever transcript exists, so a bad five minutes doesn't cost the whole interview."

stages.name: Detect it
stages.html:
Signal Means
interim interval ≫ ~300 ms slow
final latency rising slow
confidence < threshold sustained bad
VAD speech + empty transcript bad (also: Hinglish on en-IN)

stages.name: Don't hang the turn
stages.html: • Watchdog: no utterance for 4 s → bridge line; 10 s → polite close and reschedule flag.

stages.name: Fail over or degrade
stages.html:
Prove it — the ladder ():

Step Action Cost
1 repeat request one turn
2 second STT provider (warm socket, same keyterms) words in flight; a different vocabulary behaviour
3 text fallback in-session modality changes; recorded
4 scripted close + resume offer interview split

Alternatives named in the design: a second STT vendor (Gnani) as the concurrency alternative.

stages.name: Say something honest
stages.html: • "Sorry, I'm having trouble hearing you. Could you say that again?" Then the text offer.

stages.name: Protect the record
stages.html: • Turns written as they commit; the Panel scores the transcript that exists; the scorecard notes modality and gaps.

followUps.question: Why not run two STT providers all the time?
followUps.html: Double cost and double concurrency quota for a rare event. A warm standby connection opened on the first signs of degradation is the middle ground.

followUps.question: "Health-check the provider before each call."
followUps.html: Degradation happens mid-call. Health has to be continuous, per stream, with the breaker shared by the process.

followUps.question: 🧪 Confidence drops only for one candidate. Provider problem?
followUps.html: Probably not: their mic, network or accent. Ask to repeat, suggest headphones, offer text, and don't let the Prober read it as vagueness.

dontSay: "We restart the call on the backup provider."

spine: Why it grows within a call
real-time-systems-q18.testing: that you price the unit correctly (a minute of open session), know which meters dominate, and don't quote made-up prices.
real-time-systems-q18.trap: pricing per request, or ignoring that token cost grows through the call.
real-time-systems-q18.spoken:
"Stack the meters. STT bills per minute of audio streamed, whether anyone is speaking or not. TTS bills per character synthesised. The LLM bills per token, and in a voice loop every turn re-sends context, so cost per turn grows through the call. Then the transport and compute: SFU and relay bandwidth, and a process per call for the whole session. Voice bills on time, not requests: an idle open call still costs.

For our interviews there's a specific shape. The hot path is cheap. The analysis tier runs on every final phrase and restarts as the answer grows, so it spends more tokens than one call per answer; the design's speculative pre-generation is two to three times the analysis tokens, deliberately. And the post-call panel is several strong-model reads of the full transcript. At scale, the post-call scoring dominates unit economics, so batching it and caching the rubric part of the prompt stop being optional.

The levers: compact history — the speaker sees only the last eight messages — a smaller model for simple turns, caching fixed phrases, cutting the relay ratio, and budgets per run so a runaway call can't spend without limit.

I'd model p50 and p99 cost per interview, because a long rambling call is the tail that hurts. Prices come from contracts; the model gives quantities."

stages.name: The meters
stages.html:
Meter Unit Grows with
STT audio minutes streamed session length
TTS characters agent talk time
LLM tokens turns × context length
transport GB relayed / forwarded concurrency × relay ratio
compute process-minutes session length

stages.name: Why it grows within a call
stages.html:
Prove it — history cost without compaction (illustrative):

each turn adds ~150 tokens (question + answer)
turn n re-sends ~150·n tokens of history
30 turns: Σ 150·n = 150 · (30·31/2) ≈ 70k input tokens for history alone
with a window of the last 8 messages: ≈ 30 turns × ~600 ≈ 18k

stages.name: The levers
stages.html:
• Compact context; smaller models where quality allows; cache fixed phrases; batch panel inference and cache rubric prefixes; cut relay ratio.
  • Per-run budgets (calls and tokens) for the interview, T1 and evaluation: over budget → a fixed closing line, feedback still produced.

stages.name: Model the tail
stages.html: • Long calls, many clarifications, repeated barge-ins: the p99 interview can cost several times the median. Caps (turn limit 80, time limit) bound it.

followUps.question: What does your interview cost?
followUps.html: The model gives quantities: vendor-minutes, tokens per tier, node-hours per interview. The prices depend on contracts, and I wouldn't quote a number I haven't computed from them.

followUps.question: "Voice is expensive because of the LLM."
followUps.html: Often the per-minute meters (STT, TTS) and the post-call scoring are as large. Measure per meter before optimising.

followUps.question: 🧪 Average call length doubles. Which meters double, and which more than double?
followUps.html: STT, compute and transport roughly double. LLM history cost grows faster than linearly without compaction, because each turn re-sends a longer context.

dontSay: A price per minute you can't source.

real-time-systems-q19.testing: a layered evaluation with metrics text agents don't have, and regression on fixed inputs.
real-time-systems-q19.spoken:
"In layers, evaluated separately, because a failure in one hides in another.

The speech layer: does it hear and say the words that matter? Word error rate, but more importantly key-term recall on domain vocabulary, and for speech out, a pronunciation round trip and time to first byte. In our system that's an automated golden set: twenty sentences, three voices, gated on the categories we claim.

The conversation layer: does the call behave? Metrics no text agent has — first-audio p95, end-of-turn delay, barge-ins and false barge-ins, talk-over, echo suppressions, recovery after interruption. We log them per turn, and we have 25 scripted cases to run on a live call: interrupt mid-sentence, cough without words, pause for a second and a half mid-thought, ask for clarification, drop the network for five seconds.

The outcome layer: did it do its job? For a support bot, task completion and escalation rate. For our interviewer, it's scoring: is the score right and repeatable? We run the scorer against labelled answers with bias traps — a long wrong answer must score low, a speech-mangled correct answer must score close to its clean twin.

And it's all regression on fixed inputs, not demos: every config change runs the same inputs and compares. The gap: our inputs are synthetic; real accents and laptop mics are where it'll fail."

stages.name: Layers, evaluated separately
stages.html:
Layer Question Example metric
speech in/out right words? key-term recall, WER, lexicon round trip, TTS first byte
conversation does the call behave? first-audio p95, eou delay, false barge-in rate
outcome did it do the job? score MAE vs labels, repeatability, task success

stages.name: Speech layer
stages.html: • 24 Sep 2026: gated recall 99%, WER 1.7%, lexicon 100%, TTS first byte 319 ms (fails 300).

stages.name: Conversation layer
stages.html:
• Per turn: e2e, llm_ttft, tts_ttfb, stt_delay, eou_delay, interrupted.
  • 25 manual cases (V-01…V-53) across flow, turn-taking, integrity, robustness, post-call.

stages.name: Outcome layer
stages.html:
Prove it — first scoring run ( 26 Sep 2026, 52 answers × 3, labels provisional):

Check Result
MAE (0–10) 1.02 (target ≤ 1.0)
within ±1 54% (target ≥ 80%)
repeatability 0.05 std (target ≤ 0.5)
bias traps 12/12

stages.name: Regression, not demos
stages.html: • Fixed inputs, one change per run, baseline alongside, misses read individually, versions pinned, live failures become new items.

stages.name: What ours has and lacks
stages.html:
Has Lacks
automated speech goldens human recordings across accents
25 live cases, manual automated conversation replay
scoring goldens with bias traps human-reviewed labels; Panel agreement baseline

followUps.question: How would you automate the conversation layer?
followUps.html: A simulated caller: pre-recorded or synthesised candidate audio, timed to interrupt or pause at scripted points, driven through the real room; assert on the logged events and the stored turns.

followUps.question: "Use an LLM judge on the transcript."
followUps.html: It judges content, not the call: it can't see a 1.5 s dead air or a barge-in on the agent's own echo. And it needs its own agreement check against humans.

followUps.question: 🧪 WER improved, but user ratings dropped. What's your hypothesis?
followUps.html: Turn-taking regressed: a new endpoint setting cutting people off, or first audio slower. Check eou delay and cut-off rate before anything else.

dontSay: "Our WER is X" as the evaluation.

spine: Reduce the error at the source
Act only on committed, confirmed values
real-time-systems-q20.testing: a trust boundary between recognised speech and actions, with several cheap layers.
real-time-systems-q20.trap: passing the top hypothesis straight into a tool call.
real-time-systems-q20.spoken:
"The danger is that recognition errors are silent: the next stage gets a confident, well-formed wrong string with no flag on it. So I treat recognised speech as untrusted input to any action, and stack cheap layers.

At the source: tell the recogniser what to expect. Keyterm prompting and smart formatting help numbers come out as digits, and for a known ID format you can bias toward it. In our interview system, smart formatting is on because '300K QPS' versus 'three hundred K' changes how a claim reads.

Validate against the format: length, prefix, check digit if the ID has one, and match against known values — does this policy exist for this caller? A wrong digit usually fails the checksum or the lookup.

Confirm high-stakes slots by reading back: 'That's 4-7-1-2… is that right?' One extra turn, big error reduction. Use confidence: low confidence always confirms; high stakes confirm regardless.

Then act only on the final, committed and confirmed value, never on a partial. And for speaking it back, digits need to be spoken as digits, which is a TTS normalisation step."

stages.name: Errors propagate silently
stages.html:
audio → ASR top hypothesis → [ validate → confirm ] → tool call
                              └── the boundary: nothing acts before it

stages.name: Reduce the error at the source
stages.html:
• Keyterm prompting / format hints; smart formatting for numbers; n-best alternatives where the vendor offers them.
  • In our goldens, the numbers category is recall-only (95%), with variants accepted ("12,000" or "twelve thousand").

stages.name: Validate against the format
stages.html:
Prove it — a Luhn-style check catches single-digit errors (run with Python 3):

def luhn_ok(num: str) -> bool:
    total = 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(reversed(num)):
        d = int(ch) * (2 if i % 2 else 1)
        total += d - 9 if d > 9 else d
    return total % 10 == 0
print(luhn_ok("79927398713"))   # → True   (a valid test number)
print(luhn_ok("79927398718"))   # → False  (one digit misheard)

stages.name: Confirm high-stakes slots
stages.html:
Slot Confirm?
IDs, amounts, dates, names for an action always
low-confidence anything that acts always
chit-chat never
  • Speak digits as digits (a TTS lexicon or normaliser rule), grouped for the ear.

stages.name: Act only on committed, confirmed values
stages.html: • Side effects subscribe to committed turns, never interims; the confirmation is itself a turn.

followUps.question: Doesn't confirmation annoy users?
followUps.html: Only when it's applied to everything. Confirm what acts and what's uncertain; skip the rest.

followUps.question: "The LLM will notice the number looks wrong."
followUps.html: It has no ground truth for a policy number; a plausible wrong number looks exactly like a right one. Validation needs the format and the database.

followUps.question: 🧪 The caller says "fifteen" and the ASR hears "fifty". Which layer catches it?
followUps.html: Not a checksum if it's an amount. The read-back does ("fifty, is that right?"), and a range check can if fifty is out of range for this slot.

dontSay: "Our ASR is accurate enough."

spine: Memory must match what was heard
real-time-systems-q21.testing: that within-call memory is latency-critical, retrieval can't sit in the turn, and cross-call memory is written after the call.
real-time-systems-q21.trap: a synchronous vector search mid-turn that adds hundreds of ms to first audio.
real-time-systems-q21.spoken:
"Two horizons. Within the call, memory must be fast and complete enough to stay coherent. Across calls, it's retrieved and summarised, and written after the call, never on the hot path.

Within the call there are really three kinds of memory in our system. The conversation context for the speaker is compacted: it sees only the last eight messages, so the per-turn cost and latency don't grow through a 25-minute interview. The interview's progress is event-sourced: which questions were asked, how many probes were used, where we are in the plan — all computed from the moves the candidate actually heard, stored per turn. And the analysis results for each answer live in a per-interview context the turn logic reads.

Anything retrieved during the call must be pre-fetched: the plan, the keyterms, the candidate's profile are loaded before the first word. A search in the turn would blow the budget.

Across calls, things are written after the call: the Reviewer's per-question analysis, topic scores, and a revision ladder that moves a topic up or down. A resumed interview loads its earlier parts at the start — what was asked, the transcript — so the plan continues and the final evaluation covers every part.

And memory must match what was heard: if Rachel was interrupted, the stored reply is the truncated one, or the agent 'remembers' saying things nobody heard."

stages.name: Two horizons
stages.claim: within the call and across calls
stages.html:
Within the call Across calls
latency critical not critical
content recent turns, progress, insights reviews, scores, topic status
written as turns commit after the call

stages.name: Within the call
stages.html:
Prove it — three stores, three rules ():

speaker context   last 8 messages (RECENT_TURNS = 8)         → bounded prompt per turn
progress          fold over delivered moves, keyed by turn   → no counters to drift
insights          InterviewContext.insights[turn]            → written by T1, read by Chair

stages.name: Retrieval off the critical path
stages.html:
• Plan (by ID from the token's dispatch metadata), keyterms, profile — all before STT starts.
  • One exception, done safely: in the practice room a personal plan is written while the greeting plays, and swapped in only if no question has been asked yet.

stages.name: Across calls
stages.html:
• Reviewer → session_reviews / revision_reviews; revision rating → topic ladder; Panel → topic scores.
  • Resume: earlier parts loaded at start; Chair skips asked questions; evaluation spans all parts.

stages.name: Memory must match what was heard
stages.html: • LiveKit appends the spoken (truncated) reply to the chat context; the graph doesn't add the generated text itself.

followUps.question: Why only 8 messages? Doesn't the speaker lose context?
followUps.html: The speaker only phrases a move Chair chose; the plan and progress aren't in its prompt window, they're in state. Eight messages is enough to acknowledge and probe what was just said. The full transcript goes to post-call scoring.

followUps.question: "Use a vector store for conversation memory."
followUps.html: Within a 25-minute call, recency and structure beat similarity search, and a search in the turn costs budget. Vector retrieval earns its place across calls, if at all.

followUps.question: 🧪 The candidate references something they said 20 minutes ago. Can Rachel follow?
followUps.html: Not from the 8-message window. Chair's state knows which question it was, and the Prober reads the current answer. A summary of earlier answers in state would be the fix if it matters.

dontSay: "We keep the whole conversation in the prompt."

spine: What I'd reuse from my platform
real-time-systems-q22.testing: whether you name PHI, consent and the clinical human-in-the-loop boundary, and turn noise and vocabulary into measured design choices.
real-time-systems-q22.trap: a generic voice-agent answer that never says PHI, consent or who commits a clinical action.
real-time-systems-q22.spoken:
"First I'd clarify the users and the actions: is this patients at the bedside asking for help, or clinicians dictating and querying? And can it act — order, schedule, page — or only capture and inform? That decides everything about safety.

Constraints: protected health information is the hard one. So regional or on-premises inference, providers under a business associate agreement or equivalent, encryption in transit and at rest, redaction before anything is logged, zero-retention settings at every vendor, and consent and disclosure that it's an AI. I'd also switch off any framework's default recording; in my own system LiveKit Agents recorded to the cloud by default and we turned it off.

The design is a cascaded pipeline, because hospitals need the transcript as a record: near-field mic with echo cancellation, noise suppression and background-voice cancellation; streaming STT with keyterm prompting from a drug and procedure lexicon; a semantic turn detector; a rules layer that decides what happens and a model that phrases it; TTS with a pronunciation lexicon for drug names.

Noise: alarms, carts and other voices. Measure it — in my system a noise study showed steady noise cost only 3 to 4 points of term recall; vocabulary gaps cost far more. So vocabulary is the bigger lever: boost the formulary, validate recognised drug names against it, and confirm.

Latency: co-locate media and inference in-region, keep connections warm, stream everything.

And the safety line: clinical actions are human-in-the-loop. The assistant captures, reads back and queues; a clinician commits."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: who speaks, and can it act?
stages.html:
• Users: patients, nurses, physicians; ward vs clinic; languages.
  • Actions: inform only, capture for review, or execute (orders, pages).
  • Records: is the transcript part of the medical record?

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
Constraint Consequence
PHI in-region / on-prem inference; covered vendors; redact before logs; zero retention
latency p95 first audio ≤ ~800 ms (illustrative target)
accuracy on drug names key-term recall gated per category, measured on real ward audio
auditability transcript + action log, immutable

stages.name: Baseline design
Deep-dive: the four asks
stages.html:
Prove it — what my own platform measured, as the starting evidence ( synthetic voices, 24–26 Sep 2026):

Ask Design Evidence from my system
noise browser DSP + neural noise/voice cancellation steady noise down to 5 dB SNR cost ≤ 3–4 points of term recall
vocabulary keyterms from the formulary; lexicon for TTS keyterms took term recall 79–83% → 89%; lexicon 88% → 100% after one fix
latency in-region, warm pools, streaming cold TLS ~620 ms vs warm; region 15 vs 90 ms
privacy recording off, retention, redaction framework default recorded to cloud; turned off

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Control
wrong drug name recognised formulary match + read-back; never auto-order
second voice (a visitor) diarization signal; confirm the speaker
system down text/app fallback; never the only path to help
PHI in traces redact before write; retention on traces too

stages.name: What I'd reuse from my platform
stages.html: • LiveKit transport and turn detection; the echo guard idea (agent speech never enters the record); keyterm + lexicon goldens; a rules layer that decides and a model that only phrases; circuit breakers; text fallback as a first-class path.

followUps.question: Speech-to-speech for lower latency?
followUps.html: Not for anything that becomes a record or an action: the transcript is required, and controls live on text. Possibly for non-clinical chit-chat. See Q10.

followUps.question: "Encrypt it and you're compliant."
followUps.html: Compliance also covers who can access, how long it's kept, where it's processed, consent and disclosure, audit, and deletion across every copy — including traces and vector stores.

followUps.question: 🧪 Two drugs differ by one syllable. How do you stop a mix-up?
followUps.html: Treat the pair as a confusion set: when either is recognised, always read back with a distinguishing detail (dose, indication), and never let recognition alone commit.

followUps.question: How would you roll it out?
followUps.html: Capture-only first, with clinicians reviewing every transcript; measure term recall on real ward audio per unit; only then read-back flows; actions last, always human-committed.

dontSay: A design that places orders directly from speech.
No mention of PHI or consent.

real-time-systems-q23.testing: that the unit of fairness is a concurrent session, and isolation is chosen per tier.
real-time-systems-q23.trap: request-rate limiting on a workload whose unit is a 45-minute session.
real-time-systems-q23.spoken:
"The difference is that noisy neighbours are immediate and audible: one tenant's spike degrades another tenant's live call, and you can't retry a live conversation.

So limits are on concurrency, not request rate: each tenant gets a cap on concurrent sessions, and premium tiers get reserved capacity. That includes the vendor side: if the TTS vendor gives you 1000 streams, one tenant must not be able to take 900.

Isolation is a spectrum: a shared pool is cheap and risky; dedicated worker pools per tier protect premium tenants; dedicated infrastructure or a region for regulated tenants.

Per-tenant configuration runs deep in voice: the voice itself, prompts, vocabulary lists, pronunciation lexicon, escalation rules, data-residency region, retention. In our interview platform the rubric and its vocabulary come from the tenant's job description, so every session already loads a per-tenant keyterm list.

And every metric, log and trace is tenant-tagged, or you can't tell whose spike degraded whose calls. In our design, the business gateway scopes every GraphQL resolver by tenant, and the agent's processes are per interview, which already isolates one call's crash or blocking bug from another's."

stages.name: Noisy neighbours are audible
stages.claim: no retry on a live call
stages.html: • Shared vendor quota, shared SFU, shared worker nodes: each is a path for one tenant's load to reach another's call.

stages.name: Concurrency caps, not rate limits
stages.html:
Prove it — why rate limits miss (illustrative):

tenant A: 10 session starts/min, each lasting 45 min → 450 concurrent after 45 min
a 10/min rate limit never trips; concurrency does
cap per tenant = min(contracted concurrency, share of vendor quota)

stages.name: Isolation by tier
stages.html:
Tier Isolation
standard shared pools, per-tenant caps
premium dedicated worker pool, reserved vendor share
regulated dedicated infra / region, own retention

stages.name: Per-tenant config runs deep
stages.html: • Voice, prompts, rubric, keyterms, lexicon, escalation, region, retention; versioned and pinned per session (lexicon version and keyterm count are already stored per session in our system).

stages.name: Everything tenant-tagged
stages.html: • Metrics, logs, traces, cost per session: attribution is the difference between "the platform is slow" and "tenant B's batch started at 18:00".

followUps.question: Where is tenant isolation enforced for data?
followUps.html: In the query layer (tenant scoping on every resolver and query), never by prompt instruction. The agent loads only its session's plan, bound by the signed token.

followUps.question: "Give each tenant its own cluster."
followUps.html: Strong isolation at a cost most tenants don't need; and it multiplies vendor contracts. Reserve it for regulated tenants.

followUps.question: 🧪 One tenant schedules 300 interviews at 18:00. What protects everyone else?
followUps.html: Their concurrency cap (the rest queue or reschedule), per-tenant vendor share, and the post-call scoring queue absorbing the 300 panel jobs on spot capacity afterwards.

dontSay: "We rate-limit per tenant."

real-time-systems-q24.testing: whether you treat audio, transcript and derived data as separate artifacts with separate rules, and whether you know your frameworks' defaults.
real-time-systems-q24.trap: "no, we don't record" while a framework silently does, or forgetting traces and indexes in deletion.
real-time-systems-q24.spoken:
"We keep the transcript, not the audio. The transcript is the evidence the scores cite, so it's needed. Raw audio adds risk — it's biometric-adjacent and carries accent and timbre, which our scoring must not use — for little benefit.

And 'we don't record' has to be checked, not assumed. LiveKit Agents, by default, records sessions to LiveKit Cloud — audio, transcript, traces and logs. We turned that off explicitly. The audio and text still reach our STT, LLM and TTS vendors for processing, so their retention settings and data agreements are part of the answer, and the consent screen should name them.

Then separate artifacts with separate rules. In our prototype, the graph checkpoints — needed only during the call — are dropped an hour after it ends, 24 hours at most. Sessions with transcripts and scores are deleted after 30 days, with everything attached cascading. Profile and progress are kept because tracking over time is the point, and a person can be removed entirely. It runs every six hours.

Consent and disclosure are design elements: the greeting says it's an AI interviewer. And erasure has to reach every copy: the database, the checkpoints, and the traces — our tracing tool keeps its own copy, which still needs a retention setting."

stages.name: The answer for us
stages.html:
Artifact Kept? Why
raw audio no risk, and a scoring signal we must not use (N6)
transcript yes, retention-bound the evidence behind scores
derived: scores, reviews yes the product

stages.name: Separate the artifacts
stages.html:
Prove it — the prototype's retention policy ( retention.py):

Store Rule
graph checkpoints drop 1 h after the call ends, 24 h max; VACUUM the file
sessions + turns, insights, scorecards delete after 30 days (cascade)
auth sessions / login attempts 1 day after expiry / 30 days
profile, topic progress kept; a person can be removed
runs at startup and every 6 h

stages.name: Consent and disclosure
stages.html:
• The greeting discloses the AI (call case V-01); the consent screen should list processors.
  • Jurisdiction rules (two-party consent, GDPR, sector rules) decide what's allowed to be kept.

stages.name: Know every data flow
stages.html:
• Framework default recording: off (record=False), because otherwise every session goes to LiveKit Cloud.
  • Vendors that process audio/text: STT, LLM, TTS providers; check retention and training settings.

stages.name: Retention and erasure
stages.html: • Database, checkpoints, traces (tracing keeps transcripts; no retention set there yet), backups, any vector index.

followUps.question: Wouldn't audio help resolve disputes about scores?
followUps.html: Yes, that's the real argument for keeping it. If a customer needs it, keep audio short-term, access-controlled and separate from scoring, with explicit consent. The default should be not to.

followUps.question: "We don't store audio, so we're fine."
followUps.html: Transcripts are personal data too, and vendors may retain audio unless configured not to. The question is every copy, not just yours.

followUps.question: 🧪 A candidate asks to be deleted. List the places.
followUps.html: Sessions, turns, insights, scorecards, reviews, topic progress, profile, checkpoints, tracing, backups, and vendor-side logs if any were retained.

dontSay: "We don't record" without checking the framework default.

real-time-systems-q25.testing: constraint first, a trade you made explicitly, what you rejected, and two numbers.
real-time-systems-q25.spoken:
"The constraint was the product: an AI interviewer that holds a spoken technical interview. From the moment a candidate stops talking to the first sound of the next question, we had 800 ms at p95. Past that it doesn't feel like a conversation, and candidates answer differently.

The key decision was what owns turn-taking. The existing stack was hand-rolled WebRTC with a coturn relay, and our own endpointing design was a list of continuation words we admitted was guessed. I chose LiveKit — the SFU plus its agents runtime, self-hosted for production and LiveKit Cloud for the prototype — because it owns what actually dominates the budget: voice activity, a trained end-of-turn model, interruption handling, and one process per interview. The closest alternative was Pipecat; preferring it wouldn't have been wrong.

Inside each interview process, I split the agents by latency: rules pick the next move in about a millisecond; analysis agents run while the candidate is still talking; the real scoring happens after the call with independent assessors.

What broke taught me the most. Our first TTS benchmark read 1.3 seconds; it was the harness, discarding pooled connections — fixed, it was 319 ms. The turn detector at 0.5 seconds cut people off mid-thought; 0.8 fixed it. Speech recognition turned 'idempotent' into 'item potent', which makes a strong candidate look vague: keyterms took term recall from about 80% to 89%, and 96% on the Indian-accent voice. And the agent's own voice through laptop speakers could be scored as the candidate's answer, so there's a guard that drops it before the record.

In production: <fill: p50/p95 turn latency, concurrent sessions, one incident and what changed>."

stages.name: The decision it served
stages.html: • N1: p50 ≤ 450, p95 ≤ 800 ms endpoint → first audio. N7: every completed interview produces a scorecard. N6: no scoring from accent or voice.

stages.name: The constraint
stages.claim: two vendor stages are 80% of the budget

stages.name: Options weighed
stages.html:
Option Verdict
WebRTC + coturn, own endpointing undifferentiated work; a guessed heuristic
LiveKit Cloud vendor in the media path of an unrepeatable event
media-only SFUs the easy half
Daily + Pipecat closest alternative
self-hosted LiveKit chosen

stages.name: What I built
