spine: What I'd defend and what's open
real-time-systems-q26.testing: whether you can hold the whole system in your head, in order, and say why it's split the way it is, not just list components.
real-time-systems-q26.trap: starting with the tech stack ("we used LiveKit, Deepgram, LangGraph…"). Start with the constraint the stack serves.
real-time-systems-q26.spoken:
"It's an AI interviewer that runs a spoken technical interview, adapts its questions to the answers, and produces an evidence-backed scorecard afterwards. One constraint shapes everything: from the moment the candidate stops speaking to the first sound of the next question, we have 800 milliseconds at p95. Past that it stops feeling like a conversation.

So the system is split into four tiers, each with a different scaling axis. A small FastAPI control plane mints LiveKit tokens, creates rooms and handles webhooks; it never holds a live interview. A LiveKit SFU carries the audio over WebRTC. A LiveKit Agents worker fleet runs one process per interview, and that process holds the voice pipeline and the agent brain. And a cold path of queue workers does the heavy scoring after the call.

Inside one interview process, a turn goes like this: Silero VAD and Deepgram streaming STT listen to the candidate; LiveKit's turn-detection model decides whether they've finished or are just pausing; then the brain runs. The brain is a LangGraph graph split by latency. The hot path is an intent guard and a rules-based Chair that picks the next move in about a millisecond, then a speaker agent that says it, streamed into TTS sentence by sentence. While the candidate is still talking, a warm tier (Assessor, Prober, Sentinel) analyses the answer so Chair has an insight ready at the end of the turn.

When the call ends, two independent assessors score the full transcript, a reconciler resolves differences and a registrar writes the scorecard. In parallel, a Reviewer writes per-question feedback.

The principle I'd defend is that the design's hot path is transport, detection and synthesis, with no model generation; the honest caveat is that my prototype still has one streamed LLM call in the turn, which is the next thing to remove."

stages.name: The product constraint
stages.claim: 800 ms from endpoint to first audio
stages.html:
• N1: candidate endpoint → first TTS byte, p50 ≤ 450 ms, p95 ≤ 800 ms ( design target).
  • N7: a completed interview must always produce a scorecard; a live interview can't be re-run.
  • N6: no scoring signal from accent or voice timbre.
  • These three explain most of the architecture: N1 shapes the hot path, N7 creates the cold-path boundary, N6 turns STT quality into a fairness problem.

stages.name: Four tiers
stages.claim: split by scaling axis, not by function
stages.html:
Tier Runs Scales on Nodes
Control plane (FastAPI "Aditya") tokens, rooms, webhooks, session lifecycle requests (HPA) on-demand, small
Media (LiveKit SFU) WebRTC audio, built-in TURN tracks / connections on-demand, never spot
Agents (LiveKit Agents worker "Meghdootam") one subprocess per interview: VAD, STT, turn detection, brain, TTS concurrent interviews on-demand
Cold path (panel workers) scoring after the call queue depth (KEDA, scale to zero) spot

Fusing any two tiers forces the worse autoscaling behaviour of both. The spot rule comes from an earlier incident with the coturn relay: anything holding live media state never runs on spot nodes.

stages.name: One turn through the system
stages.claim: six stages, two of them vendor-bound
stages.html:
Prove it — the turn budget ( design):

turn detection            150–250 ms   LiveKit (vendor)
transcript → agent logic       ~5 ms   in-process
Chair selection                10 ms   ours (≈1 ms in the prototype)
text → first TTS chunk          5 ms   ours
TTS time to first byte        300 ms   TTS vendor (unverified under load)
SFU + network + jitter     60–120 ms   LiveKit
total                  530 typical / 690 p95   vs N1 p95 ≤ 800

Two vendor stages (turn detection + TTS first byte) are about 80% of it. That's where optimisation effort goes.

stages.name: The agents by latency tier
stages.claim: select in the turn, think around it
stages.html:
Tier When Who Kind
T0 every turn, ≤ 800 ms intent_guard → Chair → speaker (Chanakya) or a canned redirect rules, rules, LLM streamed
T1 while the candidate speaks, 2–20 s Assessor ∥ Prober ∥ Sentinel LLM, LLM, rules
T2 after the call, seconds to minutes Panel A ∥ B → Reconciler → Registrar, ∥ Reviewer LLM judges + code
  • Chair selects, never generates. If T1 isn't ready, Chair falls back to a word-count rule, so the candidate never waits on analysis.
  • The agent that asks never scores. Assessor's T1 score only steers; the Panel's T2 score is the one of record.

stages.name: After the call
stages.html:
• Two assessors get different framings and no shared context; the Reconciler resolves gaps over one point in favour of stronger verbatim evidence; the Registrar persists.
  • The Reviewer runs in parallel and never reads the Panel's output: per question it writes expected points, what was said, what was done well, what was missed and a model answer.
  • In the design, the cold path sits behind a queue (SQS) so a dead worker retries instead of losing the scorecard (N7). In the prototype, evaluation runs in the job process after the goodbye, with its own token budget, and publishes feedback_ready to the client.

stages.name: What I'd defend and what's open
stages.html:
Defend Open
tiers split by scaling axis the prototype's speaker is an LLM in the turn (speculative pre-generation is Phase 4)
per-interview process isolation TTS first byte under real concurrency (measured 319 ms warm, 1 stream)
ownership boundary: LiveKit owns audio, we own scoring consequences turn detector is English-only; not yet measured on Indian English

followUps.question: Why one process per interview?
followUps.html: The turn loop is soft real time on one event loop. A blocking call in analysis would stall turn-taking, and the symptom is dead air, not an error. With LiveKit Agents' job-per-process model the blast radius is one interview, and event-loop lag becomes a per-conversation metric. See Q48.

followUps.question: "LiveKit adds a network hop, so it costs you latency."
followUps.html: It replaced a hop. The path was candidate → TURN relay → server; it's now candidate → SFU → agent. The SFU forwards without transcoding, so the per-packet cost is comparable. The budget change is within noise.

followUps.question: Where's the state?
followUps.html: Live state is in the job process: LangGraph checkpoints keyed by turn (SQLite in the prototype), plus an in-memory context the warm tier writes insights into. Durable data (sessions, turns, insights, scorecards) goes to Postgres off the event loop. The design checkpoints InterviewState to Redis for crash diagnosis only; nothing in the turn loop reads it.

followUps.question: 🧪 TTS first byte turns out to be 450 ms under load. What happens to N1?
followUps.html: 690 − 300 + 450 = 840 ms at p95, over 800 ms, on arithmetic alone. The levers in order: a faster or nearer TTS region, then turn-detector tuning; nothing else in the chain is big enough to move it.

followUps.question: What would you build first with two engineers?
followUps.html: The instrument before the product: a device check and a live per-turn latency waterfall (endpoint, transcript final, selection, first audio) on a real residential connection. The phase machine and UX depend on decisions that aren't made yet; the latency number decides whether the architecture works at all.

followUps.question: How does the client know what the agent is doing?
followUps.html: The agent sets LiveKit participant attributes (interview.phase: evaluating, paused, feedback_ready; interview.hint: cant_hear) and live captions arrive as text streams on lk.transcription. Both ride LiveKit's signalling WebSocket, not a second channel we run. See Q28.

dontSay: The stack as the answer ("LiveKit, Deepgram, LangGraph, GPT").
"The LLM decides what to ask" (Chair is rules; the speaker only phrases the move).
A designed number as if it were measured.

real-time-systems-q27.testing: whether you chose on the criterion that actually moves your product, and whether you can name the cost of your own choice.
real-time-systems-q27.trap: defending LiveKit on transport speed. Packet forwarding isn't measurable inside an 800 ms budget; turn-taking is.
real-time-systems-q27.spoken:
"We chose self-hosted LiveKit: the SFU for media and LiveKit Agents as the session runtime. Not LiveKit Cloud, and not a hand-rolled WebRTC stack.

The deciding criterion was: pick the thing that owns turn-taking, not the thing that forwards packets fastest. Two stages are about 80% of our turn budget, turn detection and TTS first byte. A faster media server improves neither. What we actually needed was the agent runtime around the audio: voice activity detection, a trained end-of-turn model, interruption handling that flushes buffered audio correctly, and one process per interview. With raw WebRTC and coturn, all of that was ours to build: jitter buffers, Opus settings, TURN operation, three-buffer barge-in flushing, reconnects. None of that is where the product's value is, and all of it is where voice bugs live. Our own endpointing design was a hand-written list of continuation words that we admitted was guessed. LiveKit replaced a guess with a trained model.

Self-hosted rather than Cloud because of one requirement: a live interview can't be re-run, so a completed interview must never lose its scorecard. I didn't want a commercial vendor in that media path, and per-minute pricing on 45-minute sessions is a real unit-economics line. The whole stack is Apache 2.0 and the turn model has open weights, so we can inspect it, evaluate it on our accents, and fine-tune it if we have to.

The honest costs: it's a third system to operate, multi-node with Redis is deferred work, and the turn model is English-only by LiveKit's own statement. The closest alternative was Daily with Pipecat, and preferring that isn't wrong."

stages.name: The decision
stages.html:
• Is: LiveKit SFU (media, built-in TURN) + LiveKit Agents (job-per-interview runtime, VAD, turn detection, interruption, STT/TTS plugins).
  • Is not: LiveKit Cloud; a media-only SFU with our own agent loop; hand-rolled WebRTC + coturn.
  • The seam: LiveKit owns the conversational loop; LangGraph owns the decision made once per turn. Chair slots in where a LiveKit agent would call an LLM.

stages.name: The constraint that forced it
stages.html:
# Criterion Why it decides
1 Agent runtime, not just transport turn detection, interruption, per-session isolation are the work
2 Self-hostable, permissive licence N7: we must operate and inspect the media path
3 Turn-detection quality alternative was a guessed heuristic; affects fairness
4 Ops tax for a small team every extra service is permanent
5 Transport performance real, but nanoseconds against a 700 ms budget

Prove it — why transport speed can't be the criterion ( budget):

turn detection 250 + TTS first byte 300 = 550 of 690 ms p95  →  80%
STUN parse ~68 ns (a vendor's headline figure)  →  ~0.00001% of the budget

stages.name: What we rejected
stages.html:
Option Why not
WebRTC + coturn (status quo) all undifferentiated work; endpointing would ship a guess
LiveKit Cloud N7: vendor in the media path of an unrepeatable event; per-minute pricing (N3)
mediasoup / Janus / Pion solve transport only, the easy half
a Rust SFU/TURN vendor with fast benchmarks no agent runtime, licence unstated, self-measured benchmarks on an irrelevant axis
LiveKit media + our own agent loop viable fallback, but gives up turn detection and interruption handling
no media server, plain WebSocket loses AEC, jitter buffer, loss concealment, NAT traversal; browser AEC is our primary echo control
Daily + Pipecat closest real alternative; LiveKit's self-host story and EOU model fit better; a preference, not a disqualification

stages.name: What it cost
stages.claim: say it before they find it
stages.html:
• A third system to operate. Coturn was already that tax, and LiveKit subsumes it, but at scale it wants Redis and multi-node config. Single node is fine through Phase 3; multi-node is deferred, not avoided.
  • Upgrade cadence. Agents moves fast: pin versions, treat an upgrade like a prompt change (re-run the regression set).
  • A framework seam. LiveKit Agents has its own orchestration; LangGraph must not also own control flow. The split above is the rule.
  • The turn model is English-only (LiveKit's statement). Open weights make it evaluable and fine-tunable; "we can fine-tune" is a plan, not a result.
  • The TTS vendor in the design had no first-party plugin; the adapter is new work.

stages.name: What would reopen it
stages.html:
• Self-hosted operating cost exceeds what the Cloud licence would cost → revisit Cloud.
  • The LangGraph seam proves awkward → LiveKit for media, own agent loop.
  • The turn detector degrades on Indian English and fine-tuning doesn't fix it → a tuned fixed hangover, still inside LiveKit (the two decisions are independent).

followUps.question: Your prototype runs on LiveKit Cloud. Didn't you just argue against that?
followUps.html: Yes, and it's deliberate. The prototype uses Cloud to move fast on the parts that matter to the product (turn handling, echo, vocabulary, the brain) and for Krisp noise cancellation, which is a Cloud feature. The self-hosted decision is about production and N7. The code path is the same SDK and worker either way; what changes is who runs the SFU.

followUps.question: Why not just stream audio over a WebSocket? One candidate, one agent.
followUps.html: It attacks the premise fairly: an SFU's core value is forwarding among many peers, and we have two. But WebRTC also brings UDP transport without TCP head-of-line blocking, jitter buffering, loss concealment, adaptive bitrate, ICE for restrictive NATs, and browser-native echo cancellation. On residential Indian connections those matter more than on office fibre, and AEC alone is decisive for us.

followUps.question: Pipecat vs LiveKit Agents — what's the real difference?
followUps.html: Both are open-source voice-agent frameworks with plugin ecosystems. The difference for us was the whole-stack story: LiveKit ships SFU, TURN, client SDKs, the agents runtime and a trained turn model under one licence, self-hostable. Pipecat is transport-agnostic and pairs naturally with Daily's managed transport. Either can work.

followUps.question: 🧪 A vendor benchmark shows their SFU parses STUN 10× faster. Does it matter?
followUps.html: No. Tens of nanoseconds per packet against a 700 ms budget is unmeasurable. It matters for a high-density relay where per-packet CPU dominates cost. We run one candidate and one agent per room, and our bottleneck is a 135M-parameter turn model and a TTS vendor.

followUps.question: How do you keep LiveKit upgrades from breaking interviews?
followUps.html: Pin the version, and gate an upgrade on the same checks as a prompt change: the STT/TTS goldens, the 25 manual call cases, and latency on a real connection. The hook names in the Agents API move between releases; the division of responsibility is the stable part.

dontSay: "LiveKit is faster."
"We avoided vendor lock-in" without saying it's Apache 2.0 and self-hosted.
That Pipecat was a bad choice.

What breaks if you mix them up
real-time-systems-q28.testing: that you know which traffic is loss-tolerant media and which is ordered, reliable control, and that you didn't build a second control channel you'd have to operate.
real-time-systems-q28.trap: "audio goes over WebRTC, everything else over our WebSocket server" — in this system there is no WebSocket server of ours; LiveKit's signalling socket carries the control messages.
real-time-systems-q28.spoken:
"The rule is: media goes over WebRTC, because it's UDP-based and built for live audio — jitter buffering, loss concealment, echo cancellation. Anything that must arrive complete and in order goes over a WebSocket, because TCP gives you that for free.

Concretely there are four WebSockets and one WebRTC path. The candidate's microphone and the agent's voice are Opus over RTP through the LiveKit SFU. The client's connection to LiveKit starts with a signalling WebSocket: join, SDP, ICE candidates, reconnects. That same signalling channel carries our control messages. The agent sets participant attributes like interview.phase — evaluating, paused, feedback_ready — and interview.hint when it can't hear the candidate, and the live captions arrive as LiveKit text streams on the lk.transcription topic. The agent worker keeps its own WebSocket to LiveKit to register and receive job dispatches. And each interview process holds streaming WebSockets to Deepgram, for STT and for TTS.

The only plain HTTP call is the client asking our FastAPI control plane for a token and a room.

Why not our own WebSocket server for the control messages? Because it would be a second connection to keep alive, authenticate and reconnect, and its state could disagree with the room's. Using the room's own channel means the agent's state and the media share one lifecycle."

stages.name: The rule
stages.claim: loss-tolerant media vs reliable, ordered control
stages.html:
WebRTC (UDP, RTP) WebSocket (TCP)
Delivery late packets dropped, concealed every byte, in order
Head-of-line blocking none one lost segment stalls what's behind it
Built in jitter buffer, PLC, AEC, adaptive bitrate nothing media-specific
Right for live mic and speaker audio signalling, state, captions, server-to-vendor streams

stages.name: The channel map
stages.claim: one WebRTC path, four WebSockets, one HTTP call
stages.html:
Channel Carries Protocol
Candidate ↔ SFU ↔ agent mic audio up, agent TTS down WebRTC: Opus/RTP, DTLS-SRTP, ICE, TURN in LiveKit
Client ↔ LiveKit join, SDP, ICE, reconnect; attributes; text streams LiveKit signalling WebSocket
Worker ↔ LiveKit "available for jobs", job dispatch worker WebSocket
Job process ↔ Deepgram streaming STT (interims, finals) and TTS WebSockets, pooled per session
Client → FastAPI token, room, agent dispatch HTTPS POST

stages.name: How the client learns the agent's state
stages.html:
Prove it — the messages as the client sees them ( prototype):

participant attributes (set by the agent, read by the client)
  interview.phase = "evaluating"        → show "Preparing your feedback"
  interview.phase = "feedback_ready"    + interview.session_id → open the review page
  interview.phase = "paused"            → resumable, not evaluated yet
  interview.hint  = "cant_hear"         → user state "away": mic muted or wrong device
  interview.hint  = ""                  → cleared when speech is heard again
text stream, topic "lk.transcription"   → live caption bubbles, both speakers
  • Attributes are state, not events: a client that reconnects reads the current value instead of replaying a missed message.
  • The cant_hear hint exists because a muted mic otherwise looks like a stuck "Listening" screen.

stages.name: The contract between repos
stages.html:
• Client and server are separate repos. Once LiveKit owned signalling, the shared surface collapsed to two things: the token API (OpenAPI) and a small JSON schema for data messages.
  • Both repos validate against the mirrored schema in CI. The failure to design against is a client sending a field the agent silently ignores.
  • Open question: where the canonical schema lives (shared package, submodule or code generation).

stages.name: What breaks if you mix them up
stages.html:
• Audio over a WebSocket from a browser: one lost TCP segment stalls every frame behind it; you rebuild jitter buffering and lose browser AEC.
  • Control over a lossy data channel without acks: a dropped feedback_ready leaves the client waiting forever. Attributes avoid it because the latest value is state that survives reconnects.

followUps.question: Why do vendor streams use WebSockets and not WebRTC?
followUps.html: Server-to-server on a good network, with both ends under control. There's no NAT to traverse, no need for AEC, and the vendor APIs are WebSocket-based. What matters there is keeping the connection warm: a cold TLS connect to Deepgram from India measured ~620 ms, so connections are pooled and opened before first speech.

followUps.question: "WebSockets are real-time, so they're fine for audio."
followUps.html: Real-time delivery isn't the issue; ordering is. TCP must deliver in order, so under loss the audio stalls and then bursts. For live speech you'd rather drop a late 20 ms frame and conceal it.

followUps.question: The client reconnects mid-interview. What does it miss?
followUps.html: Media reconnect is LiveKit's (ICE restart, signalling reconnect). Attributes are re-read on rejoin, so the phase is correct. Captions sent while disconnected are lost from the live view, but the transcript of record is server-side, so nothing the scorer uses is lost.

followUps.question: Would you ever add your own WebSocket server?
followUps.html: Only for traffic that isn't tied to the room's lifecycle, like a dashboard of past interviews with live updates. For anything inside an interview, a second channel means a second auth, a second reconnect path and two sources of truth for state.

followUps.question: How is the token protected?
followUps.html: The API secret never reaches the browser: FastAPI mints a short-lived JWT scoped to one room and identity, with publish, subscribe and data grants, plus the agent dispatch so the right worker joins.

dontSay: "We use WebSockets for real-time and WebRTC for video."
That the control messages go through a server you don't actually run.

spine: What's ready before the first word
real-time-systems-q29.testing: whether you understand that a voice agent is a participant dispatched into a room, not an HTTP handler, and how the plan reaches it safely.
real-time-systems-q29.trap: "the client calls our API, which starts the agent." Nothing calls the agent; LiveKit dispatches a job when the candidate joins.
real-time-systems-q29.spoken:
"The client asks our FastAPI control plane for a token. The control plane checks the candidate owns the interview plan they're starting, names a fresh room server-side, and mints a short-lived LiveKit JWT: one room, one identity, publish and subscribe grants, and a room configuration that says 'dispatch the agent named meghdootam into this room', with metadata — the candidate ID, the plan ID, and whether this continues a paused interview. Because the metadata is signed into the token, the agent can trust it.

The client connects to LiveKit with that token. When it joins, LiveKit creates the room and dispatches a job to an available agent worker. The worker is a long-running process registered with LiveKit over a WebSocket. It has idle subprocesses that are already prewarmed — Silero VAD is loaded before any job arrives. The job lands in one of them, reads the metadata, loads the plan, builds the keyterm list for STT from that plan, and starts the session. The agent speaks first.

Two properties I wanted: the agent never arrives before the candidate, so there's no greeting to an empty room; and the plan is known before STT is configured, so the vocabulary boost is right from the first word."

stages.name: The one-line flow
stages.claim: five hops, one of them HTTP

stages.name: The token carries the dispatch
stages.html:
Prove it — what the token holds ( prototype, simplified):

identity   cand-<12 hex>            stable per person, reveals nothing
ttl        30 min                   to join, not the interview length
grants     room_join, room=interview-<8 hex>, can_publish, can_subscribe, can_publish_data
room_config.agents = [ RoomAgentDispatch(
    agent_name = "meghdootam",
    metadata   = {"candidate_id": …, "plan_id": …, "continue_from": …} ) ]
  • Server-named room for prepared interviews: a client can't pick a room name that collides with someone else's (threat model T8).
  • Ownership check first: someone else's plan returns the same error as a missing one, so plan IDs can't be probed.

stages.name: The worker and the job
stages.html:
• The worker registers under an explicit agent name, which also turns off automatic dispatch into every room.
  • LiveKit dispatches on join; the worker hands the job to an idle subprocess. #processes = #concurrent interviews.
  • Prewarm runs once per idle subprocess before any job: model load (hundreds of ms) stays off the first turn.

stages.name: What's ready before the first word
stages.html:
Step in entrypoint Why before the first turn
parse metadata → load the plan Chair needs it at turn 0
continuing? load earlier parts Chair skips questions already asked; evaluation covers all parts
build ≤ 100 keyterms from plan, topics, sections, stack STT is configured once, at session start
start the interview's model budget (calls, tokens) a runaway loop hits a hard stop, not a bill
open checkpoints, build the graph per-turn state keyed by turn

stages.name: Why it's built this way
stages.html:
• Pre-created room + separate dispatch: a worker restart between the two misses the dispatch.
  • Agent joins first: it greets an empty room, or the candidate misses the opening.
  • Plan fetched after the session starts: STT runs the first answer without the domain vocabulary.

followUps.question: What if no worker is available?
followUps.html: The candidate joins a room with no agent: the client shows "Waiting for the interviewer". In production the worker fleet scales on concurrent jobs with a max_jobs cap per worker, and capacity is kept warm; the alert is on dispatch wait time.

followUps.question: Why is the token TTL 30 minutes when interviews last 45?
followUps.html: The TTL bounds when the token can be used to join. Once connected, the session isn't cut at expiry; reconnects are handled by LiveKit.

followUps.question: Could the client just tell the agent which plan to run?
followUps.html: Then any client could run any plan against any candidate record. The plan and candidate ID travel inside the signed token, set by the server after an ownership check.

followUps.question: Where would token minting live in the full platform?
followUps.html: Open question. LiveKit has a Java server SDK, so the Spring gateway could mint tokens and the FastAPI edge might not need to exist. I'd decide at integration. The thing to watch is the edge growing features one reasonable step at a time.

followUps.question: How does resume work after a dropped call?
followUps.html: The token carries continue_from. The new job loads the earlier parts: what was asked, their transcript, elapsed time. Chair skips questions already asked, and evaluation runs once, over all parts, when the last part completes.

dontSay: "The API starts the agent."
A room name chosen by the client for a prepared interview.

real-time-systems-q30.testing: whether you know the difference between a request/response server and a long-lived stateful session, and where each belongs.
real-time-systems-q30.trap: "we run each interview in a FastAPI background task" — one blocking call then stalls every interview on that worker.
real-time-systems-q30.spoken:
"Because an interview isn't a request. It's a 45-minute stateful session with a soft real-time loop inside it, and FastAPI's concurrency model doesn't give you one unit per interview. Uvicorn gives you worker processes, one async event loop each, and a thread pool for sync code. Put ten interviews on one worker and they share one event loop; one blocking STT or LLM call, or a sync SDK someone added, stalls turn-taking for all ten. The symptom isn't an error, it's dead air on ten live calls.

LiveKit Agents is built for exactly this: a worker registers with LiveKit, and each interview runs as its own job in its own process. So there are three runtime shapes on the server: the agent worker, the panel worker that scores after the call from a queue, and FastAPI. FastAPI is the one that really is request/response: it mints tokens, creates rooms, handles webhooks and serves past interviews. It's stateless, off the media path, and three to six replicas cover a thousand concurrent interviews.

The cost is more moving parts, and the thing to watch is the FastAPI service slowly growing features that belong elsewhere."

stages.name: The decision
stages.claim: three runtime shapes, only one is FastAPI
stages.html:
# Process Shape Trigger Lifetime
1 Agent worker LiveKit Agents worker job dispatch on room join one job per interview, up to 45 min
2 Panel worker queue consumer SQS message () seconds to minutes
3 Control plane FastAPI HTTP from the client milliseconds

stages.name: The constraint
stages.claim: one event loop per worker, shared by everything on it
stages.html:
Prove it — what one blocking call does to a shared loop (illustrative):

10 interviews on one uvicorn worker, one event loop
one sync call blocks the loop for 400 ms
→ every interview on that worker misses its turn deadline by up to 400 ms
→ 400 ms is half the 800 ms p95 budget, on ten calls at once
with a process per interview: the same bug costs one call 400 ms

stages.name: What we rejected
stages.html:
Option Why not
interviews as FastAPI background tasks / WebSocket handlers shared event loop; deploys kill live calls; no drain semantics for 45-min sessions
agent logic behind HTTP endpoints the voice loop calls adds a network hop to every turn, and the endpoint becomes a stateless shell around state that lives elsewhere

stages.name: What it cost
stages.claim: three processes and a scope rule
stages.html:
• Three things to deploy and observe instead of one. Two of them (agent and panel worker) are one image with a MODE switch, so they can't drift apart in version.
  • FastAPI's scope is a rule, not a guarantee: session creation, candidate lookup, scorecard reads each look reasonable. Webhooks must stay idempotent and fast (return 200, enqueue heavy work) or a webhook storm at peak becomes the bottleneck.

stages.name: What would reopen it
stages.html: • When the voice service meets the wider platform: LiveKit has a Java SDK, so the Spring gateway could mint tokens and the FastAPI edge could disappear. Or the edge ships as a third MODE of the same image instead of its own deployment.

followUps.question: Couldn't you use asyncio.to_thread for blocking calls and stay in FastAPI?
followUps.html: That's a discipline we apply inside the agent process too. It doesn't fix the structural problem: interviews on one worker still share a loop, deploys still kill them, and there's still no drain for a 45-minute session. Isolation by process makes the discipline a mitigation instead of the only defence.

followUps.question: "FastAPI is async, so it handles thousands of concurrent connections."
followUps.html: Thousands of idle connections, yes. Not thousands of soft real-time loops doing VAD on 30 ms frames and streaming to three vendors each. Concurrency isn't the same as isolation.

followUps.question: How do you deploy the agent without killing live calls?
followUps.html: Session pods get a long termination grace period (3600 s) to drain live calls; the panel workers want the opposite (30 s, die fast). That opposite deploy shape is one reason they're separate workloads. The prototype sets a 120 s shutdown timeout because evaluation runs in the shutdown hook, which is the N7 risk the queue fixes later.

followUps.question: Where does session state live, if not in FastAPI?
followUps.html: In the agent job process (graph checkpoints keyed by turn, in-memory insights) and in Postgres for anything durable. FastAPI reads Postgres to serve past interviews; it never holds a live one.

dontSay: "FastAPI can't scale."
That the choice was about Python vs another language.

spine: The six stages after the endpoint
real-time-systems-q31.testing: a per-stage budget with owners, and whether you know which work happens before the endpoint so it isn't on the clock.
real-time-systems-q31.trap: starting the clock at "the candidate speaks" or quoting one total number.
real-time-systems-q31.spoken:
"The clock starts at the endpoint, the moment the system decides the candidate has finished, and stops at the first audio byte reaching them. Our target is 450 ms at p50 and 800 at p95.

A lot happens before the clock starts. While the candidate is speaking, Deepgram streams interim transcripts every 300 ms or so, and each final phrase kicks off the warm tier — Assessor, Prober, Sentinel — debounced and restarted as new phrases arrive. So by the endpoint, there's usually already an insight for this answer.

Then six stages. The turn detector confirms they're done: 150 to 250 ms, model inference plus a short silence. The transcript reaches the brain in-process, about 5 ms. The intent guard and Chair pick the move: rules, about a millisecond, 10 in the budget. The text goes to TTS in sentence-sized chunks, 5 ms. The TTS vendor produces the first audio: 300 ms target. And the SFU, network and jitter buffer add 60 to 120. That's about 530 typical, 690 at p95. Two stages, turn detection and TTS first byte, are 80% of it.

Where my prototype differs: the speaker agent is still an LLM that phrases the move, so model time-to-first-token sits inside the turn. From India that measured around 850 ms for every OpenAI model we tried. LiveKit's preemptive generation starts it before the endpoint is confirmed, which hides part of it. Removing it with speculative pre-generation is the next step."

stages.name: Where the clock starts
stages.html:
• N1: endpoint → first TTS byte, p50 ≤ 450 ms, p95 ≤ 800 ms ().
  • The endpoint is a decision (the turn detector's), so part of its cost is inside the budget: the silence it waits for.
  • Everything that can run during speech must run during speech.

stages.name: What already happened during speech
stages.html:
During speech Cadence Result
Deepgram interims ~300 ms live captions, preemptive generation input
Final phrase → T1 (Assessor ∥ Prober ∥ Sentinel) debounced 300 ms, restarted on each new phrase insights[turn] ready by the endpoint, often
Diarization labels per phrase second-voice signal for Sentinel

stages.name: The six stages after the endpoint
stages.html:
Prove it — the timeline ( design budget):

t (ms) Event Owner
0 last word; silence begins candidate
150–250 turn detector commits the turn LiveKit (VAD + EOU model)
+5 final transcript into the graph in-process
+10 intent_guard → Chair selects the move ours, rules
+5 first sentence chunk dispatched ours
+300 first TTS audio byte TTS vendor
+60–120 SFU forward, network, jitter buffer LiveKit
530 / 690 first sound at the candidate (typical / p95)

stages.name: Where the prototype differs
stages.claim: one LLM call is still in the turn
stages.html:
Design Prototype
Speaker Chair picks a pre-rendered NextMove; no generation Chanakya (LLM) writes a short acknowledgement, then the planned question verbatim
LLM in the turn none one streamed call; OpenAI TTFT ~850 ms from India (, network-bound)
Hiding it speculative pre-generation during speech LiveKit preemptive generation: starts before end-of-turn is confirmed, discarded if speech continues
Endpoint wait 150–250 ms min_delay 0.8 s (0.5 s cut thinking pauses)

The honest statement: the prototype does not meet the design budget, and I can name the two reasons.

stages.name: How I measure it
stages.html:
• Every agent turn logs e2e, llm_ttft, tts_ttfb; every user turn logs stt_delay and eou_delay (end-of-turn delay).
  • The alert: endpoint_to_first_byte p95 > 800 ().
  • Latency claims come from a real connection, never localhost: local runs omit the SFU hop and residential networks.

followUps.question: Which stage would you attack first?
followUps.html: The biggest controllable one. In the design, TTS first byte (verify the vendor's real number under load, then region). In the prototype, the in-turn LLM call, by moving generation into speech time.

followUps.question: Raise min_delay from 0.8 s to 1.2 s. What changes?
followUps.html: Every turn that ends on a "finished-sounding" utterance waits 400 ms longer before the endpoint, so median latency rises by up to 400 ms. In exchange, fewer thinking pauses get cut into two turns. It's the cut-off vs latency trade, and it should be decided on measured cut-off rates, not feel.

followUps.question: "Just use a faster LLM."
followUps.html: We measured ~850 ms TTFT for every OpenAI model from India, and LiveKit's inference gateway wasn't faster: it's network-bound, not model-bound. The fix is structural: don't generate inside the turn.

followUps.question: Why does network sit at the end and not the start?
followUps.html: The uplink happens during speech. What's on the clock after the endpoint is the downlink of the first audio: SFU forward, the internet path to the candidate and their jitter buffer.

followUps.question: How would you show a hiring panel this works?
followUps.html: A live per-turn waterfall on a real residential connection: endpoint fired, transcript final, move selected, first audio. It's the Phase 1 exit criterion, and it's worth more than any UI.

dontSay: "About half a second" with no breakdown.
That the prototype has no LLM in the turn.

real-time-systems-q32.testing: whether you'll own a gap between your design and your code, and whether you understand speculative pre-generation well enough to say why it's hard.
real-time-systems-q32.trap: defending the contradiction ("it's only a small call"). Concede first, then show you know the way out and why you sequenced it later.
real-time-systems-q32.spoken:
"You're right, and it's the main deviation from the design. The design's rule is that nothing in the turn generates: the warm tier drafts two to four candidate next moves from partial transcripts while the candidate is still talking, fully rendered and ready for TTS, and at the endpoint Chair just picks one, in about ten milliseconds. The reason is arithmetic. Human tolerance for silence is around 800 ms, and a model call from India measured about 850 ms to first token by itself. It can't fit.

The prototype keeps Chair as pure rules, but the speaker agent, Chanakya, is an LLM that phrases Chair's move. On an ask move I constrained it hard: it may write a short acknowledgement — dropped if it's over ten words or contains a question — and then the planned question is spoken verbatim, so scoring stays valid. For probes and clarifications it phrases the Prober's hint. Two things hide the cost: LiveKit's preemptive generation starts the speaker on the transcript before the endpoint is confirmed and discards it if the candidate keeps talking, and sentence chunking lets the first sentence reach TTS while the rest is still being generated.

Why not build speculation first? Because it depends on things that weren't defined: what counts as a speculative 'hit', the phase machine, the steering algorithm. Building it before those exist means rebuilding it. The cost is that the prototype doesn't meet the design budget, and I say so."

stages.name: Concede it
stages.claim: the prototype has one streamed LLM call per turn
stages.html:
Design Prototype
Chair selects among pre-rendered NextMoves selects a move kind by rules (~1 ms)
Text written during speech by the warm tier written in the turn by Chanakya, streamed
Guard "if generation enters the §10 table, the design has regressed" known deviation, documented in hot_path.py

stages.name: Why the design forbids it
stages.claim: the budget doesn't fit a generation call
stages.html:
Prove it — the arithmetic:

design turn without generation     ~690 ms p95
measured OpenAI TTFT from India    ~850 ms  (network-bound; LiveKit Inference no faster)
690 − 10 (Chair) + 850             ≈ 1,530 ms if generation were fully on the clock
N1 p95 target                         800 ms
  • The design's answer: speculative pre-generation. T1 produces a ranked set of NextMove objects (utterance, targets, confidence, generated_for_turn) during speech; Chair picks with a staleness and confidence check.
  • The fallback ladder when nothing fresh exists: best speculative move → next plan-order question → a bridge utterance that buys ~1.5 s.

stages.name: What the prototype does instead
stages.html:
• Constrain the output: on ask, the LLM writes only an acknowledgement (≤ 10 words, no question mark) and the planned question follows verbatim. The plan, T1 and the Panel all assume that exact question was asked.
  • Overlap: preemptive_generation starts the brain on the transcript before end-of-turn is confirmed; if the candidate continues, the result is discarded. Every graph write is keyed by turn and overwritten, so a re-run is idempotent.
  • Chunk: the first sentence (or 12 words) goes to TTS as soon as it exists.
  • Only the speaker speaks: LangGraph runs with stream_mode="custom", so only text a node writes through the stream writer reaches TTS, never an internal classification call.

stages.name: What it costs today
stages.html:
• Median turn latency above the design target, dominated by model TTFT.
  • Preemptive generation wastes tokens when the candidate keeps talking; it's a cheap version of speculation, without ranking or confidence.
  • Every turn depends on the LLM provider being up. A circuit breaker makes an outage fail fast instead of waiting on timeouts, but the prototype has no model-free speaker yet; the design's answer is the plan-order question and the bridge utterance, which need no generation.
  • On an ask, the acknowledgement is buffered (a few words) so it can be checked before anything is spoken. That's a small, deliberate latency cost for scoring validity.

stages.name: The path out
stages.claim: speculation, with a defined hit metric first
stages.html:
1. Define speculative_hit_rate. The cheap definition (a move passed staleness and confidence checks) and the meaningful one (a human would have chosen it too) differ; pick before building.
  2. Move Chanakya's phrasing into T1: render the utterance for the likely next moves during speech.
  3. Chair selects; the speaker node becomes a lookup.
  4. Exit criterion ( Phase 4): hit rate ≥ 70% and the turn budget met on a residential connection.

followUps.question: Speculation generates 2–4 moves and throws most away. Isn't that wasteful?
followUps.html: Yes, deliberately: 2–3× the T1 tokens. The waste buys the only thing that makes the system feel like one fast interviewer. If the unit economics come back badly, the answer is fewer candidates per turn, not abandoning speculation. The cost is unquantified today, and that's an open item.

followUps.question: How do you stop a stale speculative move being spoken?
followUps.html: Each move carries generated_for_turn and a timestamp; Chair rejects moves for an older turn or past a staleness limit. Barge-in invalidates all pending moves, because the context shifted.

followUps.question: Why not a smaller, faster model for the speaker?
followUps.html: The measured TTFT was network-bound, the same across models. A smaller model on a nearer endpoint (the design uses Groq in-region) helps; removing generation from the turn helps more.

followUps.question: 🧪 The candidate says one more sentence after preemptive generation started. What happens?
followUps.html: The turn isn't committed, so the preemptive result is discarded and the brain runs again on the longer transcript. The graph write for that turn is overwritten, not appended, so there's one move per turn in the record.

followUps.question: Would you ship to real candidates like this?
followUps.html: For practice interviews, yes: slightly slow turns cost little. For hiring decisions, I'd want the budget met, because a slow interviewer changes how candidates answer, and that's a fairness question.

dontSay: "There's no LLM in the hot path" about the prototype.
"It's only one call."

real-time-systems-q33.testing: whether you know VAD, endpointing and turn detection are different things, and whether your settings came from evidence.
real-time-systems-q33.trap: "we use a 500 ms silence timeout". No fixed hangover works for people who pause to think.
real-time-systems-q33.spoken:
"Three different signals. Silero VAD answers 'is there speech in this 30 ms frame'. Endpointing answers 'has this utterance ended'. Turn detection answers the harder question: 'has this person finished their turn, or are they pausing to think'. We use LiveKit's end-of-turn model for that: a small transformer that reads the recent words together with the audio. 'I'd shard by tenant.' is finished; 'I used Kubernetes for the…' is not, even after the same silence.

The settings: wait at least 0.8 seconds of silence when the turn sounds finished, and up to 3.5 seconds when the model thinks they're mid-thought. We started at 0.5 seconds and it cut people off at thinking pauses, so we raised it.

Vendor endpointing in Deepgram is off. Two end-of-turn authorities would fight, one committing a turn the other thinks is still open. Deepgram still gets a finalize signal when VAD says speech ended, so the final transcript arrives on time.

That's a deviation from LiveKit's own advice, which is STT endpointing by default. We accept it because the semantic model is the better trade for an interview, where long pauses are normal. The weak point: the model is English-only by LiveKit's statement, and we haven't measured it on Indian English yet. The fallback is a tuned fixed hangover, not a return to hand-written transport."

stages.name: The decision
stages.claim: a semantic end-of-turn model, one authority
stages.html:
Signal Question Ours
VAD speech in this frame? Silero, ~1 ms per 30 ms chunk, prewarmed per process
Endpointing did the utterance end? vendor endpointing off (endpointing_ms=0)
Turn detection (EOU) did the turn end? LiveKit model: 135M params (SmolLM v2 base), ~50 ms inference, four-turn window (LiveKit)

Prove it — the prototype settings, annotated ():

turn_detection = TurnDetector()          # audio + words, "finished" vs "pausing"
endpointing    = { min_delay: 0.8 s,     # silence before a finished-sounding turn commits
                   max_delay: 3.5 s }    # longest wait when the model says "mid-thought"
stt.endpointing_ms = 0                   # one authority; plugin still sends Finalize on VAD end

stages.name: The constraint
stages.claim: no fixed hangover works, and cut-offs are unfair
stages.html:
Fixed hangover Effect
150 ms fast, interrupts anyone who pauses to think
250 ms still cuts mid-sentence pauses
500 ms+ never interrupts, feels slow and dead

In an interview, cutting a candidate off mid-thought isn't only a UX problem: the split answer reads as vaguer to the scorer, and vagueness is what the Prober probes. That makes it a fairness issue.

stages.name: What we rejected
stages.claim: a guessed heuristic and double authority
stages.html:
• v0.1 design: an adaptive hangover driven by a hand-written list of continuation words. Our own open questions flagged the list as guessed, not derived from recorded speech. Withdrawn.
  • STT endpointing (LiveKit's default recommendation): simpler, but the vendor decides on acoustics and punctuation alone, and running it alongside the EOU model gives two authorities.
  • Endpointing tuned per question type ("expect a long pause after 'my policy number is'"): useful in task bots; the semantic model gets most of it from the words.

stages.name: What it cost
stages.html:
• English-only (LiveKit): no published data on Indian English or Hinglish. Open weights mean we can evaluate and fine-tune; nobody has measured it yet.
  • Turn splits still happen. A live test cut "backend engineer" at a pause ("I'm Prathap, a / pen engineer"). Chair treats a paused answer as one answer (the warm tier re-analyses all committed turns since the last full reply), so a split costs a restarted reply, not a skipped question.
  • 0.8 s is slower than the 150–250 ms the design budget assumes. It's the right trade for thinking pauses, and it moves latency.

stages.name: What would reopen it
stages.html:
• Measure cut-off rate (a turn followed within a second by more speech from the candidate) by accent cohort. If the model degrades on Indian English and fine-tuning doesn't fix it, switch to a tuned fixed hangover; the transport decision doesn't change.
  • If median turn latency matters more than cut-offs for a product (a support bot), revisit STT endpointing.

followUps.question: Is barge-in also governed by the turn detector?
followUps.html: No. Barge-in runs on acoustic onset (VAD, 0.4 s of voice while the agent speaks). A candidate interrupting must be heard whatever they're saying. Turn detection governs turn completion, not interruption.

followUps.question: "Just make the silence timeout adaptive."
followUps.html: That was our first design, and the rules were a guess. Adaptive on what? The signal that separates "finished" from "pausing" is mostly in the words and prosody, which is what the model is trained on.

followUps.question: 🧪 A candidate says "um…" and pauses 2 seconds. What happens?
followUps.html: VAD sees silence; the model reads "um…" as unfinished, so it waits past min_delay, up to max_delay 3.5 s. If they resume within that, it's one turn. Past 3.5 s the turn commits, and the next reply, if they keep talking, is re-analysed as part of the same answer.

followUps.question: How do you measure whether the setting is right?
followUps.html: end_of_turn_delay per turn in the logs, the cut-off cases in the manual call suite (V-22), and a cut-off rate by cohort. The fairness version of the metric is the one that decides.

followUps.question: Why is the model's language support a fairness issue and not just quality?
followUps.html: Because cut-offs aren't random: they fall more on speakers the model wasn't trained on, and a cut-off answer scores worse. A model trained on the wrong distribution still beats a heuristic trained on nothing, but it has to be measured per cohort, not assumed.

dontSay: "VAD tells us when they've finished."
That the English-only limit is solved.

spine: Decide what the move was worth
Treat the answer as one answer
real-time-systems-q34.testing: that you know the framework handles the audio, and that you own the bookkeeping: what the candidate actually heard, and what that means for the plan and the score.
real-time-systems-q34.trap: stopping at "we stop the TTS". The hard part is the record afterwards.
real-time-systems-q34.spoken:
"Detection is on sound, not words. LiveKit's interruption handling in VAD mode fires when there's at least 0.4 seconds of candidate voice while Rachel is speaking. Waiting for a transcript would add 200 to 300 ms, and the candidate would hear Rachel talk over them.

The framework then stops consuming the TTS stream and flushes the audio already queued, so the tail doesn't keep playing, and it appends to the conversation what was actually spoken, truncated and marked interrupted, not what was generated.

The bookkeeping is ours, because it has scoring consequences. Chair tracks progress as a fold over moves the candidate actually heard. An interrupted probe or clarification didn't happen: it doesn't spend the probe budget and doesn't advance the plan. An interrupted ask counts only if the planned question itself was fully spoken before they cut in — if only the acknowledgement's tail was lost, they heard the question. Everything the candidate says after the last move they heard is treated as one answer, so a barge-in doesn't split their answer into fragments the Assessor scores separately.

Finally, not every sound is an interruption. If no words arrive within two seconds — a cough, a desk tap — Rachel resumes where she stopped and no candidate turn is created. Backchannels under 0.4 seconds, like a short 'mm-hm', don't trigger it at all."

stages.name: Detect on sound
stages.claim: VAD, 0.4 s, while the agent is speaking
stages.html:
• Why not the transcript: it arrives 200–300 ms after the sound. By then the agent has spoken over the candidate.
  • Why 0.4 s: long enough to ignore a short backchannel or a click, short enough to feel responsive.
  • Mode: vad, not LiveKit's adaptive (an ML model that ignores backchannels). vad makes barge-in predictable and visible while tuning; adaptive is the candidate for production once measured.

stages.name: Stop the audio
stages.html:
Buffer What's in it Action
TTS stream audio still being synthesised stop consuming it
outbound pacing buffer audio synthesised but not yet sent flush
client playout audio already sent the stream ends; nothing new arrives

v0.1 of our design specified this sequence by hand. It's the class of detail that's easy to get subtly wrong, so it's now the framework's.

stages.name: Record what was heard
stages.html:
Prove it — two turns in the stored shape (illustrative text):

turn 7  assistant  "That makes sense. How would you shard the led…"   interrupted=1
turn 8  user       "Sorry, one second — by account id, and…"          interrupted=0
  • The history holds what was heard, not what was generated.
  • The design goes further: record the exact character offset reached in the TTS stream, so the Assessor never penalises an answer to a question that wasn't fully asked.

stages.name: Decide what the move was worth
stages.html:
def delivered(move, spoken, plan):          # 🔧 hot_path.py, abridged
    done, text = spoken                     # (spoken to the end?, text heard)
    if done or move["kind"] == "greet":
        return True
    if move["kind"] == "ask":               # did the planned question itself get said?
        return norm(plan[move["q"]].question) in norm(text)
    return False                            # interrupted probe/clarify: didn't happen
  • Progress is event-sourced: probes used, questions asked and the current question are all computed from delivered moves, never from counters.
  • In the design, barge-in also invalidates the pending speculative moves, because the context they were drafted for has changed.

stages.name: Treat the answer as one answer
stages.claim: merge since the last heard move
stages.html:
• answer_since(last_delivered_turn) joins every candidate turn since the last move they heard.
  • The warm tier re-analyses the whole merged answer when each turn commits, and resets only when a reply was heard in full.
  • Without this, one answer split by a barge-in would be scored as two thin answers.

stages.name: Tell noise from interruption
stages.html:
Event Behaviour () Test
cough / tap, no words agent pauses, resumes within 2 s (false_interruption_timeout) V-21
"mm-hm" under 0.4 s ignored V-23
"Sorry, one second" audio stops within ~0.5 s, turn stored interrupted=1 V-20

Metric: false barge-in rate. Most conversational tuning assumes peers; an interviewer holds the floor longer.

followUps.question: What if the "interruption" was the agent's own voice through the speakers?
followUps.html: Then it's echo. Barge-in fires on sound before any transcript exists, so the echo guard can't prevent the interruption, only keep the echo out of the record. That's why client-side AEC is primary. See Q35.

followUps.question: "Log the full response; the model generated it."
followUps.html: The next turn's context and the scorer would then assume the candidate heard words they never heard. The conversation record must match what was said aloud.

followUps.question: Should the interrupted LLM call be cancelled too?
followUps.html: Yes, or you pay for tokens nobody hears. The framework stops the generation along with the audio; in the design there's no generation in the turn to cancel, only pending moves to invalidate.

followUps.question: 🧪 The candidate interrupts after the planned question was fully said, during a trailing "take your time". Does the question count?
followUps.html: Yes. delivered checks that the planned question's text is inside what was spoken. They heard the question; only the tail was lost, so the plan advances.

followUps.question: Would you ever disable barge-in?
followUps.html: For fixed lines where interruption would break something: the prototype's closing line after a time or budget stop is said with interruptions off, because the call is ending either way. Never for questions: a candidate who can't interrupt can't ask for clarification.

dontSay: "We detect interruptions from the transcript."
"The full response goes into history."

spine: Why echo is a scoring bug
Layer 1, cancel it in the browser
Layer 2, drop it before the record
real-time-systems-q35.testing: whether you see echo as a correctness problem in an interview product, and whether you know why a server-side check can protect the record but not the conversation.
real-time-systems-q35.trap: "WebRTC has echo cancellation, so it's handled." AEC misses, and a miss is silent.
real-time-systems-q35.spoken:
"Candidates use laptop speakers as often as headphones. If Rachel's voice leaks back into the mic, every downstream stage misreads it: turn detection thinks the candidate is talking, barge-in cuts Rachel off, STT transcribes her words as the candidate's, and the Assessor scores our own question as their answer. That last one is a scoring-validity bug, not an annoyance.

So there are two layers. The primary control is the browser's acoustic echo cancellation, on in the capture settings with noise suppression and gain control, mono. It's primary because only the browser has the far-end reference — the exact audio being played — so it can predict the echo and subtract it.

Behind it, a server-side echo guard. When a candidate turn ends while Rachel is speaking or within 1.5 seconds of her stopping, we compare its text with what Rachel just said. If at least 80% of the candidate's words appear, in order, in Rachel's text, and it's at least three words, we drop the turn before it's committed. It never reaches the brain, the transcript store or the Panel.

The honest limit: the guard can't prevent an echo-triggered interruption. Barge-in fires on sound within about 150 ms, and the transcript it needs arrives 200 to 300 ms later. So AEC protects the conversation; the guard protects the score."

stages.name: Why echo is a scoring bug
stages.html:
Stage What echo does
turn detection sees speech: "the candidate is talking"
barge-in fires: Rachel stops mid-word
STT transcribes Rachel's words as the candidate's
Assessor / Panel scores our question as their answer

stages.name: Layer 1, cancel it in the browser
stages.html:
• getUserMedia with echoCancellation, noiseSuppression, autoGainControl, mono, through the LiveKit SDK.
  • AEC learns an adaptive filter for how the speaker output arrives back at the mic and subtracts the prediction; a double-talk detector freezes adaptation while both talk, so the candidate's voice isn't cancelled.
  • It needs 3–4 s to converge, so the most echo-prone moment is the opening line. The device check should play throwaway audio first so the filter converges before the first real question.

stages.name: Layer 2, drop it before the record
stages.claim: a string check, not a classifier
stages.html:
Prove it — the containment score the guard uses (run with Python 3):

import re
from difflib import SequenceMatcher
norm = lambda s: " ".join(re.findall(r"[a-z0-9']+", s.lower()))
def containment(user, agent):
    u, a = norm(user), norm(agent)
    m = SequenceMatcher(None, u, a, autojunk=False)
    return sum(b.size for b in m.get_matching_blocks()) / len(u)
agent = "Tell me about a backend system you designed and the trade-offs you made."
print(round(containment("a backend system you designed and the trade offs", agent), 2))  # → 1.0
print(round(containment("I designed a payments ledger on Postgres", agent), 2))           # → 0.42
  • Rule (): drop when containment ≥ 0.8, the turn ends while the agent speaks or within 1.5 s after, and it's ≥ 3 words. The drop is StopResponse in on_user_turn_completed, before the turn is committed.
  • Containment, not similarity: the leaked fragment is usually a part of the agent's sentence, so "how much of the user text is inside the agent text" is the right measure.

stages.name: What the guard can't do
stages.html:
t (ms) Event
0 Rachel's voice leaks into the mic
~150 barge-in fires on sound; Rachel stops
~350–450 the transcript exists; the guard says "that was us" and drops the turn

The candidate has already heard Rachel cut herself off. That's why AEC is primary and the guard is defence in depth.

stages.name: The weak spots
stages.claim: partial leaks and the caption flash
stages.html:
• A candidate on laptop speakers in a hard-walled room can leak partial overlap that verbatim containment won't catch. If echo_suppressed_total runs high, headphones become a hard gate ().
  • The live caption may flash the echo briefly, because STT text streams to the browser before the turn ends.
  • Other mitigations from the literature we don't have yet: ducking agent audio during speech and headphone detection.

followUps.question: Why not do AEC on the server?
followUps.html: The server doesn't have the far-end reference as the candidate's speaker actually played it: device delay, room acoustics and volume are all on the client. Browser AEC has the playback signal locally.

followUps.question: 🧪 The candidate echoes part of the question back. Will the guard drop it?
followUps.html:
It depends on the overlap, and the rule can misfire. Against the question above, run through the same function:

"So you want the trade-offs of the ledger design?"   → 0.6   kept
"the backend system I designed"                       → 0.93  dropped, if within 1.5 s

The second is a real answer opening that the guard would drop, because the score is computed on characters and the candidate reused Rachel's words. The time window and the 3-word floor limit it; the measurement is suppressed turns reviewed by hand. If false drops show up, compare on words, not characters, and raise the floor.

followUps.question: "Just require headphones."
followUps.html: It's a fairness and access cost: some candidates don't have them. We recommend them in the device check and only make them mandatory if measured echo rates demand it.

followUps.question: Does Krisp noise cancellation help with echo?
followUps.html: Partly. BVC is trained to keep one primary speaker and mask background voices, so a faint leaked voice can be suppressed. It isn't an echo canceller and has no far-end reference; don't rely on it for this.

followUps.question: How would you know if echo is hurting scores in production?
followUps.html: Two counters and a join: echo_suppressed_total and barge_in_total{source="suspected_echo"} per session, joined against device type (speakers vs headset). A high rate in one cohort is a fairness finding, not just a UX one.

dontSay: "The guard prevents echo interruptions."
"WebRTC handles echo."

spine: Why a wrong term is unfair
real-time-systems-q36.testing: that you know a mangled term is a scoring error, not a cosmetic one, and that you fixed it with measurements rather than a word list you hoped would work.
real-time-systems-q36.trap: "we boost keywords" with no numbers and no limit. Boosting can't create a word that wasn't said, and the list has a cap.
real-time-systems-q36.spoken:
"A garbled technical term isn't a neutral error. If a candidate says 'idempotent' and the transcript says 'item potent', the Assessor sees someone who can't name the technology they claim to know. So vocabulary is a fairness problem.

On the listening side we use Deepgram Nova-3's keyterm prompting: up to 100 terms per session, given to the model as context, which biases decoding toward those spellings when the audio is ambiguous. The list is built per interview in priority order — the plan's own terms first, then the topics in play, curated terms for the section, the candidate's stated stack, and a 66-term backend base list — because the cap cuts from the end.

On the speaking side there's a versioned pronunciation lexicon: 23 entries, so Rachel says 'Kubernetes' for k8s and 'E T C D' for etcd. The transcript keeps the original text; only the spoken form changes.

We measured it on a golden set. Keyterms took term recall from 79–83% to 89% on US voices, and the production config reached 96% on the Indian-accent voice; on the categories we claim, 99% recall and 1.7% word error rate. The lexicon went from 88% to 100% on a round-trip test after one fix: 'et C D' was being heard as 'that CD'.

The last line of defence is the LLM: the Reviewer and Panel are told the transcript comes from speech recognition, and they reconstruct 'item potency keys' as idempotency keys from context."

stages.name: Why a wrong term is unfair
stages.html:
Heard Transcribed without keyterms Effect on scoring
idempotent "item potent" candidate looks vague
GraphQL "BRAFQL" claim unreadable
Raft "RAF" wrong technology
OOM killed "UAM killed" incident story garbled
cache "cash" nonsense

( real errors from the golden set, 24 Sep 2026)

stages.name: Listening: keyterm prompting
stages.html:
• Nova-3 takes plain terms as context; there are no per-term boost weights (the (term, boost) shape is Nova-2 keywords). Deepgram caps it at about 500 tokens.
  • It only breaks ties toward your vocabulary. It can't produce a word that wasn't said and can't beat very unclear audio.
  • Loaded at session start, so it applies from the first interim, not only to finals.

stages.name: Which 100 terms
stages.claim: priority order matters because the cap cuts from the end
stages.html:
# Source Example
1 the plan's own terms (JD, topic mock, revision) functools.wraps
2 topic names in play Decorators
3 curated terms per section (Python, DSA, LLD, HLD, Cloud, Java, React) useEffect, p99
4 the candidate's stated stack FastAPI, Postgres
5 base backend list, 66 terms Kafka, idempotency

Mocks without topics boost HLD first: a live noisy test heard "p99" as "page 99" when only Python terms were boosted.

stages.name: Speaking: the pronunciation lexicon
stages.html:
• 23 entries, version lex-2026-09-24.2; the session record stores the lexicon version and keyterm count, so any transcript traces back to its config.
  • Applied in the TTS path only (after sentence chunking, on complete words); the transcript keeps "k8s".
  • Reviewed, not auto-generated: a wrong entry is worse than the engine's default guess.

Prove it — the improvement loop, one change per run ():

Run Change Effect
1 63 keyterms, lexicon v1 lexicon 88%: etcd heard as "that CD"
2 etcd → "E T C D" lexicon 100%
3 + OOM, cache, queue keyterms gated recall 96% → 99%

stages.name: The last line of defence
stages.html:
• The Reviewer's and Panel's prompts say: the transcript is from speech recognition; ignore accent, grammar and filler; judge content.
  • Live test: transcript "Item potency keys" → Reviewer's did well: "Mentioned idempotency keys for safe retries".
  • This rescues the analysis, not the transcript. The stored evidence quote still shows the slip.

stages.name: What we measured
stages.html:
• Terms left out of the list: 50% recall. That category is reported, not gated, because it shows what the list can't do.
  • All numbers are from synthetic, studio-clean speech; they overstate accuracy against a laptop mic.

followUps.question: Why not just put every technical term in the list?
followUps.html: The cap (~100 terms, ~500 tokens), and dilution: biasing toward hundreds of rare words raises the chance of hearing one that wasn't said. The priority order puts the terms this interview is about first.

followUps.question: How does a new term get added?
followUps.html: A miss on a live call becomes a new golden item, the term is added, the suite re-runs with the old config beside the new one, and the version is bumped. Read the misses, not the averages: "item potent" says add a keyterm; "that CD" says fix a lexicon entry; an empty transcript says language mode.

followUps.question: 🧪 WER went down but a candidate still got scored as vague. How?
followUps.html: WER counts every word equally. One wrong "the" and one wrong "etcd" cost the same, but only one changes the evidence. That's why key-term recall is the gated metric, and semantic (meaning-weighted) WER is the better proxy than raw WER.

followUps.question: Where should the term list come from long-term?
followUps.html: The rubric compiler: it already knows the competencies from the job description, so it can emit the STT terms and pronunciation candidates in the same pass. The lexicon stays human-reviewed.

dontSay: "Keyword boosting fixes accents."
WER as the only metric.

real-time-systems-q37.testing: whether a decision that sounds exclusionary was measured, and whether you know exactly who pays for it.
real-time-systems-q37.trap: "most candidates speak English anyway." That's an assumption; the answer is a measurement and a named cost.
real-time-systems-q37.spoken:
"We run Deepgram in Indian English, en-IN, not the multilingual code-switching mode, and we decided it with numbers. On the same golden set, multilingual mode did capture Hinglish — 'hamne Kafka use kiya tha' came back — but technical-term recall fell from 86% to 76%. In a technical interview, words like idempotent, etcd and GraphQL are the evidence. A mangled term makes a strong candidate look vague, which is its own unfairness. Multilingual mode also returns mixed Latin and Devanagari script, which breaks the English keyterm list, the scoring prompts and the verbatim evidence quotes a recruiter reads.

The voice side agrees: the TTS vendor's Hindi voice is weak, so a Hinglish-speaking interviewer would sound worse.

So the interview is conducted in English and says so up front; Hinglish is tolerated, not supported.

The cost is real and I'd say it first. On en-IN, Hinglish doesn't come back garbled, it comes back empty. The words silently vanish, which is worse than a bad transcript because nobody sees it. The mitigation — detect 'VAD heard speech but the transcript is empty' and ask the candidate to repeat in English — is designed, not built. Candidates who code-switch more pay this cost, so it belongs in the per-cohort fairness audit. And the numbers come from synthetic voices."

stages.name: The decision
stages.claim: en-IN, English-only, stated to the candidate
stages.html:
• STT language = en-IN with keyterm prompting ( decided 24 Sep 2026).
  • The interview says it's in English at the start; Hinglish is tolerated (non-goal in v1: multilingual interviews).

stages.name: The measurement that forced it
stages.html:
Prove it — same golden set, two modes ( synthetic voices):

en-IN + keyterms multi + keyterms
English technical-term recall 86% 76%
Hinglish captured no (empty transcript) yes
Script Latin Latin + Devanagari mixed
Keyterm list, scoring prompts, evidence quotes work disrupted

stages.name: What we rejected
stages.html:
Option Why not
multi mode for everyone 10 points of the metric that decides technical scores
detect language per turn and switch model mid-call STT is configured per stream; switching adds a reconnect and a gap, and the scoring prompts still see mixed script

stages.name: What it cost
stages.html:
• Hinglish on en-IN → empty transcript. A candidate who explains a key idea in Hindi loses that answer unless they repeat it.
  • Mitigation: VAD speech + empty transcript → Rachel asks them to repeat in English. Not built.
  • Code-switch category in the golden set: 50% (reported, not gated).
  • Numbers are synthetic; human recordings may move them.

stages.name: What would reopen it
stages.html:
• A role whose working language is Hindi.
  • A multilingual model that closes the term-recall gap, measured on the same golden set.

followUps.question: Isn't this unfair to candidates who think in Hindi?
followUps.html: It has a fairness cost, and I'd rather own it than hide it. The alternative moves the unfairness to everyone whose technical terms get mangled. Both are fairness costs; we picked the one that protects the evidence technical scores depend on, told candidates up front, and put code-switching into the cohort audit.

followUps.question: Why is an empty transcript worse than a wrong one?
followUps.html: A wrong transcript is visible: a reviewer can spot nonsense. An empty one leaves no trace. The candidate thinks they answered; the scorer sees silence.

followUps.question: 🧪 A candidate says "we used Kafka kyunki throughput bahut high tha". What does the transcript hold on en-IN?
followUps.html: Probably the English fragments, like "we used Kafka", with the Hindi parts missing, or nothing. The claim survives; the reasoning ("because throughput was high") doesn't, and reasoning is what the Prober probes for.

followUps.question: How would you build the repeat-in-English mitigation?
followUps.html: Track VAD speech duration per turn against transcript length. If there was over a second of speech and the transcript is empty or near-empty, Chair picks a clarify-style move ("Could you say that again in English?") and the turn is marked, so the cohort audit can count how often it fires and for whom.

dontSay: "Nobody speaks Hinglish in interviews."
That multilingual mode "doesn't work" (it works; it costs term recall).

real-time-systems-q38.testing: whether you check the measurement before the system, and whether you can tell a small miss on a gate from a budget failure.
real-time-systems-q38.trap: switching TTS vendors over 19 ms without asking whether the number is right, or whether it's measured under the conditions that matter.
real-time-systems-q38.spoken:
"First, trust the measurement. Our first TTS benchmark read 1.3 seconds, and the system was fine: the harness abandoned streams midway, which discarded the pooled connection, so every later measurement paid a cold connect. Once it drained every stream, warm p50 was 319 ms. So I always suspect the harness first.

Second, is 19 ms the problem? The 300 ms line is one slice of an 800 ms p95 budget, and 319 is warm p50 on a single stream. The real risk is what it becomes under concurrency and at p95, which we haven't measured. If it's 450 under load, the budget fails on arithmetic.

Third, what's already done: sentence chunking with a 12-word forced flush, one TTS stream per segment started immediately, and warm pooled connections. The flush alone cut first audio on a long unpunctuated sentence from 677 to 437 ms. And the cold connect, about 620 ms from India, only hits the first turn.

The options, in order: try the vendor's nearest region, try a faster engine like Cartesia or ElevenLabs Flash or the design's Smallest.ai, or accept 320 and rebalance the budget. The rule: decide on p95 under target concurrency, not on warm p50 of one stream."

stages.name: Trust the measurement first
stages.claim: the harness bug that read 1.3 s
stages.html:
Run Harness Read
before abandoned streams mid-way → pooled connection discarded → every later stream paid a cold connect ~1.3 s
after drains every stream to the end 319 ms warm p50

A measurement bug, not a system change ( 24 Sep 2026).

stages.name: Is 19 ms the real problem?
stages.html:
Prove it — what the number does to N1 ( budget):

p95 budget with TTS at 300    690 ms
TTS at 319                     709 ms   still under 800
TTS at 450 under load          840 ms   fails N1 on arithmetic
  • The gate says FAIL; the budget says fine at one stream. What's unmeasured is p95 at 500–1000 concurrent streams.

stages.name: What's already optimised
stages.html:
Technique Measured effect
12-word forced flush + one stream per segment, started at once 32-word unpunctuated sentence: 677 → 437 ms first audio
warm pooled connections cold connect ~620 ms paid on the first turn only
fallback voice (OpenAI TTS) after one retry availability, not speed

stages.name: The options
stages.html:
Option Buys Costs
vendor's nearest region network RTT from India may not exist
a faster engine (Cartesia, ElevenLabs Flash, Smallest.ai) possibly 100+ ms new adapter (Smallest.ai has none), voice change, re-run lexicon goldens
accept ~320 and rebalance nothing to build less margin for residential networks
cache fixed phrases (greeting, closing, redirect) ~0 ms first byte on those turns only helps fixed text

stages.name: The decision rule
stages.html:
• Load-test TTS at 500 and 1000 concurrent streams; decide on p95 first-byte.
  • Keep the golden harness in the loop for any vendor change: TTFB, lexicon round trip and MOS-style listening checks.

followUps.question: Why one TTS stream per segment instead of one stream per reply?
followUps.html: LiveKit's Deepgram TTS sends Flush only when the whole reply ends, so a long first sentence would hold back the first byte for the whole generation. Per-segment streams let segment 1 synthesise while segment 2 is still being generated; pooled connections make them cheap. LiveKit also deprecated multiple segments per stream.

followUps.question: 🧪 What does the chunker do with a 25-word question and one full stop at the end?
followUps.html: Two flushes: 12 words, 12 words, then the final word with the full stop. A one-word tail segment is fine for latency but can sound clipped, which is one reason to prefer punctuation in generated text.

followUps.question: "Warm p50 is what users experience."
followUps.html: Users experience p95, on the first turn too, under whatever concurrency the vendor is serving. Warm p50 of a single stream is the most flattering number available.

followUps.question: Who owns this decision?
followUps.html: It's a product decision with a cost line: TTS is 55% of the budget and a per-minute cost. I'd bring the p95-under-load numbers, the voice quality comparison and the price per minute, and let the budget owner choose.

dontSay: "We'll switch vendors."
A TTFB number without saying warm or cold, p50 or p95, and how many streams.
